Madam Speaker, I am pleased to present a petition regarding section 745 of the Criminal Code.
If one is convicted of first degree murder the penalty is life imprisonment without eligibility for parole for 25 years. Under section 745 of the Criminal Code an inmate can apply for a reduction in the number of years of eligibility. In effect a convicted murderer can be released after serving only 15 years of incarceration. So life does not mean life when one is convicted of first degree or second degree murder.
The petitioners request that the Parliament of Canada eliminate or remove section 745 of the Criminal Code which allows for this reduction in the parole eligibility for first degree murderers and second degree murder.

Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to table this morning, pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The first one is from a very large number of petitioners in British Columbia who are concerned that the environmental assessment and review process guidelines passed by Order in Council on June 22, 1984 require that a public review be held of any federal activity where there is significant potential adverse effect or public concern about the proposal.
The petitioners therefore call on Parliament to urgently conduct a public environmental review of the federal policy of allowing nuclear powered and/or nuclear armed vessels in Canadian waters and harbours. The examples are Dixon Entrance, Georgia Strait and the harbours of Nanoose, Esquimalt and Halifax.
May 13, 1993

Madam Speaker, the second petition is from a large number of British Columbians from my constituency who are concerned about the link that has been shown to exist between violence and entertainment and desensitization to violence in society.
They are particularly concerned about the culture of violence demonstrated in the serial killer board game, a game which comes with a bag of 25 babies. The point of the game is to murder as many defenceless children and adults as possible.
Since the laws of Canada do not deal with banning the sale of these materials portraying torture, rape and murder, the petitioners call upon Parliament to amend the Criminal Code of Canada so that violent and degrading materials such as the serial killer board game cannot be distributed in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a number of petitions on behalf of 236 residents of my riding of Cochrane-Superior; more specifically the residents of Homepayne, Longlac and Hearst. The residents of this area are greatly concerned about the possible closure of the northern railway line.
The petitioners have grave concerns about the devastating impact on the lives of the workers, the citizens and the communities along this line in northern Ontario.
The petitioners therefore call upon Parliament to reaffirm that the Canadian National Railways will continue to have rail service in northern Ontario, and specifically retain the northern line.

That this House regrets that, despite many grand announcements in international forums and despite the passage of two and one-half years since the launch of the green plan, the government has failed

to integrate fully environmentally sustainable development as a goal
of public policy.
She said: Madam Speaker, to begin my comments this morning, I am going to quote from the minutes of the environment committee of the House of Commons earlier this week. The quote is from our witness, Mr. Jim MacNeill, who was among other things secretary-general of the Brundtland commission which produced the report Our Common Future that led ultimately to the conference in Rio earlier this year.
One quote from Mr. MacNeill demonstrates clearly the reason for this morning's motion. He said: "The gap between our international rhetoric in Canada and our domestic policies is growing wider, not narrower. If more of the committee's recommendations had been acted upon, I think the reverse would have been the case. Canada would now have brought some of its truly perverse domestic policies in line with our truly advanced environmental rhetoric and Canada would be in a much more effective position to provide strong and credible international leadership".
We have indeed had some superb rhetoric from the government over the last five years in particular that I have been here, and pitifully little action in my view.
I want to quote Mr. MacNeill because I think he had the faith of the committee. This is fundamental to why we have seen so little action, why our climate continues to disintegrate, why we continue to have fundamental inadequate legislative programs to protect our water, our land and the survivability of life on this planet.
Mr. MacNeill said: "I have been struck by the fact that our leaders always find it easy to embrace environmental rhetoric under the guise of principles and then support continuing processes of conferences, studies and negotiations under the guise of action. As a political strategy it is a proven success but as a strategy for a transition to more sustainable forms of development or environmental protection it leaves just about eveiything to be desired".
Canada likes to boast of having excelled at the earth summit in Rio and indeed we did play an important role. I think our leadership on the biodiversity convention and to some extent our leadership on the climate change convention helped ensure that this was the largest attended conference by heads of state ever in the history of the world, particularly when the President of the United States having to some extent without collaboration destroyed the climate change convention that meant anything and would accomplish anything finally did,

May 13, 1993
Supply
nonetheless, attend the conference and that was important.
When we look to the substance again we have done veiy little. Nearly a year after the earth summit Canada has set in place a number of processes. We have our new project de societe where people come together and talk. I do not undermine the importance of that because it is important for many segments of society to become partners, to become co-actors in solving our environmental problems because the sources of the problems are varied and the solutions are varied.
When all we have is process we are betraying our obligation to future generations to leave them a world in which they can live. We have failed totally on some specific environmental issues but much more fundamentally we have failed to integrate environment and development.
We often talk about sustainable development as integrating the environment and the economy. It is much more than that. The Brundtland commission gave us the concept of sustainable development and described it as a three-legged stool. It is economy. It is environment. It is people. It is human development as well as economic development.
We are far from that in this country. We have no approach yet to policies that automatically and routinely assess their impact on the environment, the impact on depletion of resources, the impact on overconsumption of resources and the impact on increasing poverty that leads to continuing the spiralling of environmental degradation. These simply are not ingrained yet in how we make decisions in every single area.
Let me talk about some specific areas in which action is needed and has not taken place and try to demonstrate how failing to act in these vital areas is important to protecting life on the planet. It is betraying our hopes for an economically prosperous future. It is also betraying the hopes of two-thirds of the world's people who live in poverty so that we can prosper in the industrialized world.
On global climate change we know that our atmosphere is deteriorating to the point where life on earth may no longer be possible. We know drastic action is needed now to reduce the damage we are doing. Yet the best the international community was able to come up with and the best Canada as a national policy has been
able to come up with is stabilizing our emissions at 1990 levels.
This is not now, not today, but seven years from now. We know that is not adequate. We know a growing population on the planet will in a very short period of time demand six times the energy that is now consumed if existing patterns of development are followed. We know consumption and emissions from fossil fuel consumption are destroying the atmosphere.
I do not think I need to tell anybody who has been out in the sun so far this year that we have a serious problem over the northern hemisphere of ozone depletion this year. There are actions to be taken to further reduce the damage we are doing to the ozone layer that have not been taken by the Government of Canada.
We signed biodiversity conventions at Rio. Yet we have not in place the policies and the plans to protect habitat. We know very little about the species of the globe, even in our own country. We have taken no action to collect that knowledge or to even begin to understand what it is we need to protect. When immediate issues come up like preserving Clayoquot Sound, one of the largest remaining original old growth forests on the face of the earth, our federal government fails to take any action.
On more important issues such as international poverty I have seen no sign that we have even started to understand the depths of the problem, that we have even started to understand we are impoverishing the poorest of the world by our lifestyle, our trade policies and our aid policies.
We know that 3.5 million children die from lack of something as basic as clean water. We know that we continue as the richest countries in the world not to give but to take $52 billion from the poorest of the world. What does that have to do with the protection of the human environment?
People who are struggling barely to subsist, to survive, destroy forests to grow food. They accept our exports of toxic wastes for jobs. They continue to export their raw resources to us and give up the means of their own development and the means for their own people to move out of poverty.
We have done something so obscene in this country that I really cannot believe it has actually been a policy that has come out of this government without ever being debated in Parliament. We have done something perverse in taking money away from those who are most in need in this world and transferring it to develop trade with the eastern bloc countries. What we have done is

May 13, 1993
ensure that the developing world will continue to grow poorer and poorer so that trade can grow richer and richer. Trade is a very important component of development, of alleviating the terrible disparity between those in this world who have and those who have not, which is the disparity between the ability to live and the certainty of dying.
Trade that is going to create a better world is not trade that exploits, that wants to sell to the poorest but not buy from them, or that wants to remove raw resources from the poorest parts of the world and sell manufactured goods back.
If trade is going to be part of equalizing the opportunities in this world, of a fair sharing of the resources of the world and through that protecting the resources of the world, it has to be two-way trade. It has to be trade which recognizes that the continuing impoverishment of most of the world is not going to lead to long-term prosperity for any of us.
We have the NAFTA now and it is going to be debated in the House very shortly. The principles of the NAFTA have never been debated in the House. Yet as I watched the hearings of the committee, the committee at the instruction of the government is so narrowly focused on small, technical considerations in the bill that we have not even had the opportunity to look at what its impact on sustainable development will be, or what its impact on the environment will be.
Frankly we have not had very optimistic signals from the government on this whole matter. We were told back when NAFTA was being negotiated that the federal government was trying to negotiate in environmental considerations. Yet now that we have a government in the United States that wants to do just that we have a Minister for International Trade who suddenly does not want that at all.
I want to quote from an interview with the Minister for International Trade a couple of weeks ago in which he was asked about the environment. His answers said very clearly that the government wants to be free to violate its own environmental regulations. It wants the sovereignty not to protect the environment and that is why it does not want these agreements. He said: "Well let's just take the environment. We have had rules that have been put in place by the Government of Canada on the Oldman River in Alberta where we did something else, i.e. we did

not obey those rules. We applied those rules in a way that we thought was appropriate. The courts turned around and said no. They thought it was inappropriate. The point I am making here is that you and I can have a very honest disagreement on something and if it is applied to international trade law it can lead to trade sanctions if you disagree with the way I have done something".
The minister was very clearly saying that the government does not want environmental considerations in a trade agreement because it does not want to have to abide by environmental legislation if it becomes inconvenient.
Madam Speaker, I am going to ask for your guidance here because the clock is not working and therefore I have no way of knowing-

speechtext: You have four minutes.

I have four minutes left. It is obvious that four minutes is a short time to do justice to the issues involved with looking at the world in a whole new way and realizing that any economic prosperity we have depends on our natural resources, any social development we have depends on our natural resources and we are in a crisis.
As Mr. MacNeill said to the committee, we await disasters before we do anything about problems. He mentioned the ecologically based famines in Africa, the last oil spill off the Shetlands, water shortages and the collapse of the fisheries, about which we in Canada know well.
Surely we do not have to wait for an imminent disaster to act. Surely we want to work toward harmony between the environment and the economy so we can continue to live and prosper on this planet.
I want to briefly quote from a speech made a few months ago by the hon. Leader of the Opposition. He spoke about governing in the 1990s. He said: "One principle of governing in the 1990s is understanding that social policy, economic policy and environmental policy are and must be linked. Without ensuring the long-term health of our environment we threaten the basis of our livelihood. Environmental protection must be a central preoccupation of all governments. A Liberal government will put in place a sustainable development policy to improve the quality of our environment. A major nation-

May 13, 1993
Supply
al industrial priority of the Liberal government will be to give Canadians the competitive edge by focusing on the promotion and development of new Canadian environmental technologies. These will form the basis of new industries and new jobs and will create a new market for Canadian goods and services".
It is time to realize that doing what is good for the environment is also doing what is good for our economy and for humanity. An industry that is more efficient, consumes less energy, dirties less water and inputs fewer chemicals is a more efficient and more competitive business, not a less efficient and less competitive business. If we do not recognize that we will find that our products will become both unaffordable and unacceptable in international markets.
If we do not recognize that with the largest coastline in the world we have an opportunity to develop water technology, clean-up technology and disaster prevention technology that we can market to the world, we are doing a disservice to the world and to our future.
Madam Speaker, I see you giving me the sign that my time is up. I have many colleagues who wish to embellish specific aspects of this issue. In closing I would like to say, again citing Mr. MacNeill, that our leaders at Rio left almost nothing unsaid and almost everything undone. We as the opposition party preparing to take power in this country after the next election want to reverse that. We want to focus on action. We want to truly make Canada a leader in sustainable development.

Madam Speaker, in relation to the final concluding remarks of the member who just spoke, she raised during her speech the issue of Clayo-quot which is a very controversial issue in British Columbia.
As the member would know, on April 6 an open letter to Canadians was sent by a number of Canadians, including myself and the Conservative chair of the Standing Committee on the Environment, the hon. member for Rosedale, and the former Minister of the Environment, the hon. member for Davenport, encouraging the Government of British Columbia to place the
issue of Clayoquot in core. It was signed by Pierre Berton, Farley Mowat and others.
Within a matter of a few hours the hon. member, along with the official spokesperson for the Liberal Party on the environment, the hon. member for LaSalle- Emard, put out a press release saying that all of Clayoquot should be added to Pacific Rim National Park.
Since that time neither she nor the Liberal spokesperson, the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard, have given any interviews or speeches in British Columbia on this proposal, nor have any of the more than a dozen Liberal members of the B.C. legislature raised such a proposal.
The member ended her remarks by saying that the Liberals are now preparing to become the government. What will the position of the Liberal Party be on the issue of Clayoquot should it be elected the government?
Is it the position that was enunciated in the press release, which has not been modified or retracted, that all of Clayoquot should become part of Pacific Rim National Park?

Madam Speaker, the member made a couple of comments and I would like to respond to them.
The member described the process around Clayoquot Sound quite accurately. As he will know, the opposition Liberal critic on the environment and myself were invited to sign the same letter. We concluded after discussions with the leader's office that a process response to the imminent recommencement of logging at Clayoquot Sound, to put it into another process, was not the answer. There needs to be a concrete resolution.
He is perfectly right that the B.C. members have given lots of interviews but I have not heard them raise the issue in this House while we have raised the issue directly with the minister and the premier of British Columbia. Our members in B.C. are free to raise it in the House if they wish. Our position is in writing to the Minister of the Environment and the premier of British Columbia.

Madam Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague from Ottawa West for her commitment to the environment and all those very important questions. I am particularly impressed by the link she makes between the deteriorating
May 13, 1993

environment, the deteriorating quality of life and the increase in poverty.
Without trying to be unkind I am trying to summarize some of the points that have been made with regard to the government's position. Please correct me if I am wrong. I will not be offended.
There has been a lot of talk, discussion and rhetoric but little action. Certainly the substance is missing. It seems to me as well-and the member may have addressed this and I did not pick it up-there is uncertainty. As I recall $3 billion was set aside over five years, and that has been reduced. Now it is over. If I am correct then that creates significant uncertainty.
I wonder if my colleague could respond to that and to the fact it is back loaded. By that I mean a lot of that money was supposedly going to be spent during the last five or six years, depending upon the figure, but we have no assurance that is going to happen because we have no assurance the government will be in power.
It is a little bit like the budget. We are going to save this many billions of dollars but we are going to save it over six or seven years or whatever the figure. We do not know that to be true because we do not really believe this government is necessarily going to be there.
A final brief comment. Whether we talk about pollution in the air, soil or water, it seems to me there has been a lot of discussion and a lot of promises made but little action. I would just like to focus for a moment on water pollution.
I do not say it unkindly but as I understand it there has been very little work done by the Minister of the Environment with respect to the cleaning up of the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes. I wonder if my colleague knows anything about those particular issues. Perhaps she would like to clarify and help me understand.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my colleague raising the issue of the green plan. There is one fundamental provision in the green plan, if it were implemented, that would move us much further along than we are right now. That is the commitment that any policy going to cabinet would be accompanied by an environmental assessment. We were told two years ago it was already being done and that when any policy was
Supply
tabled an environmental report based on that assessment would be tabled at the same time.
We have just had the budget, a major policy document of any government, with no environmental assessment. We have just had the legislation on preventing marine disasters tabled, with no environmental assessment and no information on its environmental impact.
On the question of money, it really is one of do you or do you not put your money where your mouth is, and the cuts have been dramatic. From an initial commitment in 1990 of $3 billion over five years that should have been $600 million a year, it has been reduced to the point that less than one-third of that was committed to year one and less than one-third was committed to year two. We are creeping up to a little over half that amount for year three. As was said, the government has never admitted it has backed off from that commitment whatsoever, but it just keeps putting it off to further and further into the future. Clearly the commitment is minimal if the resources and plans are not there to carry it out. It is all just words.
The Great Lakes is one of the greatest treasures of this world. It is 20 per cent of the entire fresh water supply. We have treated this area like an open sewer. As Mr. MacNeill said to the committee, we are great on rhetoric, on adopting principles and on setting process in place. That is exactly what we have done to the Great Lakes: regional action plans, areas of concern, meetings, conferences but there has been very little progress.
We have identified and now know we have to prevent damage and we cannot afford to keep cleaning it up. Even to clean up the damage we have done would be useless unless we stop what created it in the first place. Even with new legislation controlling effluents from pulp and paper mills, well over half the effluents are still allowed into the Great Lakes and other rivers and lakes across the country. We know the effluent in and of itself is entirely a toxic substance, but we still allow it to be pumped into our waterways legally. In the process we endanger not only a valuable Canadian resource but an invaluable global resource in the Great Lakes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this important debate today. Hopefully in doing so I can bring some concrete information to the House and to those who might be

May 13, 1993
Supply
watching which does establish there has been a great deal of federal action as a result of the green plan and more is under way.
The government released its report on the second year of the green plan a few short weeks ago on March 29. This report is part of our regular reporting process which helps Canadians to be effective partners in the green plan's implementation and evolution.
The second year report reviews progress on a number of long-term green plan goals and summarizes action taken to fulfil green plan commitments. It previews plans for year three. It also provides information on financial requirements by department and by program. As the year two report shows, real progress has been made on implementing sustainable development in Canada and various indicators show the green plan is making headway, despite what may have been heard. Some 80 federal initiatives and programs are under way. These touch aspects of life affecting virtually all Canadians from the air we breathe and the water we drink to the food we eat.
For example, the federal government has signed sustainable agricultural agreements with the provincial governments of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Ontario and Alberta. Other agreements are presently being negotiated.
Land has been set aside for a new national park on Baffin Island. An agreement was signed to establish Aulavik National Park on Banks Island in the Northwest Territories. Feasibility studies are under way for parks in Manitoba and northern Labrador.
The National Parks Act was amended on June 18 providing authority for the formal establishment of Gwaii Haanas National Park, a national marine park reserve in Queen Charlotte Islands providing for the co-operative agreement with the Haida nation. An agreement was reached with the president of the Council of the Haida Nation on the joint operation of the park.
The first ever joint meeting of Canada's parks, wildlife and environment ministers was held in Ottawa in November. At that meeting all participants signed a statement of commitment on protected spaces.
Seven cost shared agreements were concluded to stabilize, restore and interpret threatened historic resources of national significance. The agreements made for the operation of these national historic sites by partner agencies include the Walker Theatre in Winnipeg; the Old Stone Church in Beaverton, Ontario; Victoria Town Hall in Petrolia, Ontario; the CP Station in Winnipeg, Manitoba; Morrin College in Quebec City; the Church of Our Lady of Good Hope in Fort Good Hope, Northwest Territories and the McLean Mill in Port Albemi, British Columbia.
On June 25 the location of 10 proposed forest sites to make up Canada's model forest network was announced. Each of these model forests will be managed and funded through a partnership agreement between Forestry Canada and the model forest partnership group.
Phase two of the St. Lawrence action plan to which my hon. friend was just referring has been recently announced. In phase one the plan achieved a 74 per cent reduction in discharges of liquid toxic effluents into the river by 50 of the most serious polluters. That is a very important accomplishment.
Other accomplishments are the conservation of 5,000 hectares of wildlife habitat along the St. Lawrence, the creation of a marine park in the Saguenay River and the implementation of recovery plans for six threatened species, including the beluga.
The Wild Animal and Plant Protection and Regulation of International and Interprovincial Trade Act was granted royal assent. In addition recovery plans were completed for seven endangered migratory bird species. These and other measures will help conserve wild species, especially endangered ones, thus carrying out the provisions of the global convention on biological diversity adopted at Rio.
The Energy Efficiency Act was passed, licensing was expanded of R-2000 energy efficient houses and 10 model homes are being constructed. These initiatives will foster the development and commercialization of new technologies for energy efficiency.
May 13, 1993

In February 1993 the environmental citizenship messages program was launched through Environment Canada's weather offices to inform Canadians about global warming and the actions they as individuals can take to help meet the challenge of global warming. This program is being expanded to include messages on water, waste, species, spaces and various regional issues.
The global warming science program is now determining the rate, extent of regional distribution and socioeconomic impacts of global warming in Canada.
Canada's ozone layer protection program is achieving results. As of June 1992, CFC consumption had decreased by 58 per cent since 1986.
In March 1992 Environment Canada's atmospheric environment service introduced Ozone Watch, a weekly bulletin of up-to-date information on the status of the ozone layer over Canada. In May of the same year Canada became the first country to introduce daily ultraviolet index bulletins, giving information on the maximum levels expected during the day. These are two important steps which help provide Canadians with accurate and timely environmental information.
Thirty-one doctoral fellowships have been awarded, and more awards will follow as part of the effort to expand and better equip the next generation of environmental scientists.
The number of full-time inspectors and investigators has been increased from 49 to 70, to facilitate enforcement of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and the Fisheries Act and to provide consistent and effective enforcement programs across the country.
In May 1992 a federal-provincial-municipal agreement for the Fraser River was signed and a Fraser River Basin Management Board was established to develop and provide direction for the program. This board is made up of members of all three levels of government, public interest groups and First Nations.
Inspections help prevent marine spills. The percentage of foreign vessels undergoing inspection on entry into Canadian waters has been increased from 8 per cent in 1980 to 16 per cent in 1991 and to 38 per cent in 1992. The internationally agreed minimum standard for inspection is 25 per cent which we are well above.
Supply
Spill response equipment is now carried on board all Coast Guard ice-breakers. Training courses in marine response have been updated. Multi-agency marine response exercises were carried out in co-operation with the U.S. coast guard and other stakeholders.
The foregoing are some of the federal initiatives. In addition, people across Canada have been working together to make the green plan a success. For example, in Atlantic Canada 13 communities are developing blueprints for managing their coastal resources. Each project is organized and run at the local level.
In Quebec the Centre interuniversitaire de recherche en toxicologie de l'Universite de Montreal et de l'Uni-versite du Quebec a Montreal is part of a national network examining the effects of toxic chemicals on living organisms.
In Ontario the automotive industry has established a comprehensive pollution prevention project aimed at achieving voluntary reductions in the use, generation and release of toxic substances.
On the prairies working models of sustainable forestry are being developed in each province involving partnerships between governments, industry, aboriginal groups, academia and others.
In British Columbia the Fraser River sustainable development plan has brought together a wide range of partners. The plan seeks to clean up contaminated sites, prevent further pollution, restore wildlife habitat and the salmon populations, and enhance water quality. It provides a starting point for the federal-provincial-municipal agreement on the Fraser River to which I have already referred.
In the north a team of students cleaned up a 50-year legacy of hazardous and unsightly waste on the shores and islands of Great Slave Lake in a project launched by the Metis nation of the Northwest Territories.
The government and people of Canada thus are acting to implement the green plan in our country. Canada has also made a fairly high constructive contribution to the earth summit in Rio last June.
The green plan provided a general framework for Canada's participation in the summit. It also gave guidance in dealing with specific issues such as climate change, fisheries and forestry. As we implement our

May 13, 1993
Supply
green plan, Canada is providing a model to other countries that are developing their own strategies and action plans for harmonizing environmental protection and economic growth. In fact that is why Dr. Mostafa Tolba, former executive director of UNEP, was so excited with the publication of the green plan. He realized it could serve as that model.
On December 4, 1992 Canada became the first industrial nation to ratify both the global conventions on climate change and biodiversity adopted at the earth summit. These landmark agreements call for action on two pressing world-wide environmental programs.
The framework convention on climate change commits developed nations to implementing policies and measures to mitigate climate change by limiting emissions of greenhouse gases and protecting and enhancing greenhouse gas sinks. Canada has adopted a quick-start agenda for the climate change convention. Our first national report outlining the actions being taken in Canada to implement the convention, including an assessment of progress in reducing emissions, will be completed this summer.
The convention on biological diversity formally commits the world community to countering the threat posed to sustainable development by the loss of ecosystems, species diversity and genetic variability in species. The federal government is working with the provinces, First Nations, industry, environmental groups and others to develop a Canadian biodiversity strategy to be put in place by November 1994.
Canada is also furthering the cause of biodiversity in tropical countries which have the greatest wealth of animals and plants. We provided significant financial and organizational support to an international meeting on developing national biodiversity strategies which was held in Costa Rica last November.
Canada strongly supported the accelerated timetable for phasing out ozone depleting substances agreed to in November 1992 at the Copenhagen meeting of the parties of the Montreal protocol.
As we make the shift to sustainable development, the green plan recognizes we must do more than address specific environmental problems. In particular, we must
also change the decision-making process to take account of environmental factors from the outset.
For example, the Environmental Assessment Act has been granted royal assent. This legislation is a key element in the over-all strategy of ensuring that the government itself adheres to high environmental standards.
Another achievement is the code of environmental stewardship which was adopted in 1992 to be applied to all federal government operations. All federal departments, for example, are being required to comply with the code by preparing environmental action plans.
Canadian environmental groups took part in the consultations that accompanied negotiations on the North American free trade agreement and environmental issues were part of the negotiating process itself. The government conducted and released an environmental review of NAFTA, a first for an international trade agreement. In subsequent meetings of the three signatory nations we have agreed to establish a North American commission on the environment, a formal mechanism for trilateral environmental co-operation.
New pulp and paper regulations based on sound science have come into force. They require industry to introduce changes to pulp and paper processing which will prevent the formation of dioxins and furans and strictly control conventional pollutants in pulp mill effluents. The regulations mean that Canada has in place a national standard to ensure the protection of the environment and to ensure that Canadian industry continues to be internationally competitive.
A discussion paper on economic instruments was released as the first step in harnessing market forces for environmental protection.
In its first two years the green plan has achieved notable successes in cleaning up our environment. It is also making sustainable development a guiding principle linking economic development and environmental protection, both at home and abroad.
From Atlantic coastal communities to the Fraser River Valley and the shores of the Arctic, Canadians are working together to meet the green plan's goal of a cleaner, safer and healthier environment.
May 13, 1993

We can all take pride, and I believe we should, in our collective efforts and in our accomplishments. They show that Canadians are putting into practice the motto "Think globally, act locally".
The year 1992 will be remembered as the year of the earth summit, a key event in advancing the agenda of sustainable development. The summit and its decisions provided a wider context for the implementation of the green plan, one that did not exist in 1990 when the plan was launched.
The past two years have shown that the fundamentals of the green plan are as valid today as they were in 1990. However, it was conceived as a living plan, able to respond to changing circumstances and changing science. We need to ensure that the plan continues to respond to newly emerging needs and that we profit from the lessons learned.
Our first priority should be to make better use of the full range of tools available for protecting the environment. We are doing this by shifting the emphasis from the old react and cure approach to an approach of anticipating and preventing environmental problems before they occur. We can also do it by promoting voluntary action as the strategy of first resort, by harnessing market forces to influence the millions of collective and individual decisions, and by streamlining the activities of the different levels of government in Canada.
Our second priority should be to give more attention to the economic side of the sustainable development equation. The business community is a key partner and must be a key partner in the development of a new relationship between the environment and the economy in Canada. The green plan should support the emergence of an environmentally competitive private sector, one able to meet consumer demands in Canada and to gain fresh ground in international markets.
Our third priority should be to address more fully the global aspects of sustainable development. We must ensure that our international conventions work effectively. We can do this, for example, by ensuring that environmental considerations are reflected in international trading rules such as at the GATT and that is part of the present negotiations. We should also assist developing countries in their efforts to make the transition to sustainable development.
Supply
The government remains firmly committed to carrying out the green plan. However the federal government cannot solve all environmental problems alone. The continuing success of the green plan depends above all on co-operation and on partnership, because ultimately it is Canadians everywhere who will deliver on the green plan's potential.

Madam Speaker, it is unfortunate the parliamentary secretary did not directly deal with important points raised by my colleague, the member for Ottawa West, in her opening speech. However I appreciate the fact the parliamentary secretary wanted to put on record his points and themes.
I would like to ask him, if everything is proceeding so well according to schedule as the parliamentary secretary seems to indicate, whether he could answer some questions.
For instance, why has Canada not ratified the Law of the Sea Convention? Why has Canada cut back aid to the poorest nations in Africa? Why do we still not have, as promised in the green plan for 1991, a water bill? Two years have gone by since the date promised in the green paper. Why is almost every recommendation by environmental impact assessment panels from the Oldman River dam in Alberta to the Pearson airport in Ontario ignored by this government? Why is ethyl bromide still permitted in Canada while it has been banned in the United States in order to protect people's health from sun rays? Why does Canada still not have a plan for the stabilization of carbon dioxide? Why are pesticides exempt from the GST?
I will conclude this short list of questions. Why are billions of dollars still allowed by the tax system of this government to subsidize the fossil fuel industry and none is made available for the development of alternative energy, industry and resources?
Would the member care to answer perhaps a couple of these questions in the time available to him?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend-I use that term deliberately-has indeed provided a number of questions that would probably fill up Question Period for a few days if he had the opportunity to ask them.

May 13, 1993
Supply
He has had responsibility in this area at the ministerial level. I know he has had his convictions and concern for the environment for many years. This is not something that has come to him recently. He is not a new-found convert to environmental concerns as sometimes one can accuse politicians of being.
Many of the issues he addresses are not new. They are indeed as long standing as I am sure he would be prepared to say if he were speaking openly. He understands fully that many of them require a considerable period of time to be implemented. He also knows full well that some of them require a great deal of scientific research before there is a widespread consensus on which chemicals, for example, are to be permitted into a country to be utilized and which are not. In many cases these are ongoing reviews.
He speaks, for example, of the exemption of GST for pesticides. He knows that one part of the tax policy of the government was to permit businesses to recover the costs incurred in the business operation. The Canadian farm community indeed does make use of pesticides, herbicides and other chemicals. The vast majority of Canadian farmers does this with those that have been legally accepted for use in Canada. Because that is part of a required business expense for farming they are either exempted or they are recoverable, whichever the case may be.
He talks in terms of whether the government has always accepted fully the review of environmental assessment panels. He knows it is the purpose of those panels to give advice to the relevant minister, whether it is the Minister of the Environment or some other minister. That is the way the EARP guidelines were struck. These guidelines were created by the administration of which he was a part. I think that is an acceptable philosophy because indeed it is the minister who must be accountable in the end.
I would note however that sometimes there are honest differences in opinion as to the appropriateness of an environmental assessment panel review. I think, for example, of Wood Buffalo National Park where the panel in question advised that all the bison there should be destroyed. That is not a view that was shared by a lot of different groups in Canada. They had very sincere objections to that. I just use that as one example of where there are continued varying opinions on the appropriateness of an assessment.
What is important about the environmental assessment process is that it provides an opportunity where it is implemented for evidence and for opinions to be collected from all sources and for the information to be laid on the table. The principle is that it is the relevant minister who makes the choice. That is part of the political accountability required under environmental assessments and it is one with which I am comfortable.
There will on occasion be differences between what has been recommended and what the minister has subsequently done. The minister will clearly be accountable for his or her decision in that instance. I do not have too much difficulty with that principle.
On the question of water the hon. member knows the federal water policy as enunciated by the government in the past remains in effect. I would share with the hon. member a desire that the legislation to which he refers be introduced as soon as possible. It is not something that falls under the jurisdictional area for which I have some responsibility, but I would hope his wishes in that respect are met as they are my own.
With respect to the question of aid to Africa, this is an area to which his colleague has already referred. It is an area about which I as an individual member of Parliament have had some meetings with officials of CIDA. The challenge facing such agencies is how best to distribute the resources that are theirs to distribute. As the hon. member knows and as most of us know, eastern Europe has been subjected to very destructive forces in recent times. What is happening therefore is simply that the need many of us are aware of in Africa exists elsewhere as well. There is a tremendous demand for the dollars that are available.
It is important the hon. member understands, and I believe he does. He would not want anyone to misunderstand that aid continues to go to the so-called poorest countries in Africa as in the past. The food programs continue to exist as they have in the past. The need for that is self-evident. I visited refugee camps in southern Sudan, northern Kenya and briefly in Somalia as we delivered food. The need is almost beyond the ability of Canadians to comprehend. I want to ensure the hon. member understands that food aid continues to be delivered as it was before.
May 13, 1993

The hon. member is referring to the additional need for bilateral development programs. He is correct. There is a need there and the challenge facing CIDA and other departments is how to balance that need with the needs that exist in many countries in eastern Europe and elsewhere.
I have a great deal of interest in Cambodia at the moment partly for selfish reasons because my daughter is one of the UN volunteers there who is trying to help conduct an election in a few days under great difficulty. People who have an interest in Cambodia say unequivocally that country deserves more aid and that other countries in Asia deserve more aid than we are able to provide.
Our challenge is one of trying to take relatively scarce dollars and distribute them in as equitable as possible a manner. However it would be a mistake for anyone to conclude there is no further aid going to the horn of Africa. Indeed the food aid is going as it was before. The need for more aid, I readily admit, is there. It is also there in Cambodia and in parts of eastern Europe.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to enter this debate today and to start with the remarks of the member who just spoke.
We look at what is happening in the world and we come to scrutinize Canada's response since the green plan seems to be it at the moment. I reflect again on some remarks of Jim MacNeill that I raised in the House yesterday. It is a study that is under way for a book that a friend of Mr. MacNeill's is writing. The conclusion is that the 24 OECD countries are squandering $1 trillion or more a year on unnecessary subsidies within their own economies, particularly on things like fossil energy.
Many members of the House know, and probably not too many Canadians know, that the flow of resources from the developed world to the developing world has reversed in the last 24 months. As recently as 1991 there was a net flow into the developing countries or the poorest countries in the world of about $5 billion a year, particularly from northern countries. It was a north-south flow. That reversed and by the end of 1992 it was more than $5 billion the other way. We are the richest countries in the world and are extracting, at enormous human and ecological cost, capital from the poorest parts
Supply
of the world for what is already the wealthiest parts of the world.
A good friend of mine by the name of Walt Taylor who lives in Smithers has done an enormous amount of work with notable Canadian scholars and scholars from around the world in looking at how we can reverse all this and get to full employment, not just in Canada but world-wide.
It is interesting that we could provide from just the rate of subsidy squander of the OECD countries, health care, education and full employment across the planet. Yet there does not seem to be that kind of discussion going on in this post-Rio period.
Jim MacNeill did sum it up rather well when he said that the Rio rhetoric by leaders, including our own Prime Minister, covered everything but the national actions that have taken place since Rio last June have implemented almost nothing.
The debate today is a critical one because it is a question that Canadians and citizens of the world have to address. When does rhetoric become lies? I think that is something we need to reflect on.
I will spend a few moments on the green plan. The now leader of the Bloc Quebecois was formerly the Conservative Minister of the Environment. When he first talked about the green plan it was going to be $6 billion over five years. It became $5 billion over five years when the member for Berthier-Montcalm took the post and then it became $3 billion over five years.
When we looked at the research done by the parliamentary library and the Main Estimates of the Ministry of the Environment, we found it went from $3 billion over five years to that amount over six years in March 1991. The green plan was reprofiled in the February 1992 budget deferring $150 million from the 1992-93 and 1993-94 fiscal years to future years. In the mini budget of December 1992 it cut another $172 million from the green plan. During the first two years of the green plan 24 per cent less was spent than was originally promised. This year's spending is expected to be 36 per cent less.
The table in the document provided to members of the House shows that the green plan allocation for the combined fiscal years of 1991 to 1993 was cut by 18 per cent by the December 1992 mini budget. We go from $6

May 13, 1993
Supply
billion over five years to something less than $3 billion over more than she years. As we have learned only a tiny fraction of the money has actually been spent. I will come to that in a moment.
If we look at what the total budget of Environment Canada is for this year, it is a 1.5 per cent reduction from last year's estimates. The budget of the much heralded Parks Program was reduced. The Environmental Services Program was reduced.
The government continues to pat itself on the back, saying it is doing something about the 12 per cent resolution that was passed unanimously in the Elouse almost exactly a year ago now. I introduced it in the House and the it was reintroduced by the present Minister of Environment and jointly seconded by the member for LaSalle-Emard and myself. It said we would set aside 12 per cent of Canada by the year 2000. The federal government has not moved to set aside one jot, one tittle or one hectare outside the National Parks Program to achieve the 12 per cent.
I will quote from the research branch of the parliamentary library: "The green plan proposes the completion of the national parks system by the year 2000. Portions of all 39 of Canada's natural regions are to be included. To date 1.8 per cent of Canada's territory, 215,000 square kilometres, is in some way protected as a national park, national historic site or historic canals. The convention on biological diversity ratified by Prime Minister Mulroney on December 4, 1992 calls for the preservation of 12 per cent of each country's land as protected areas".
When we look at what is actually happening in terms of Canada's parks program we find the following. Plans are in progress for the development of a number of national parks. The planned expenditure for 1993-94 is $3.9 million for the whole of Canada. Aulavik is to receive $2.7 million and the Saguenay Marine Park, $924,000. This leaves only $362,400 for all the remaining projects in Canada.
Here is a government which goes to Rio: bluster, bluster, bluster, rhetoric, rhetoric, rhetoric. It comes back to Canada and says:"Yes, we are going to actively move on the 12 per cent. We are going to complete the
national parks system by the year 2000". It is telling us it is going to complete, with a budget expenditure of $362,000, all the national parks in Canada.
At some point rhetoric becomes lies. I think that is one of the tragedies of the Commons. One of the tragedies of the parliamentary institution in this country at this moment is that it has become poisonous, determined to send the right signals to voters, the right signals to the electorate, but never to make those hard decisions.
My friend from Davenport quite accurately pointed out that this government subsidizes the fossil fuel sector in this country at a rate of 100 to 1. In Hibernia and Lloydminster, for every $1 spent on energy conservation, energy efficiency, alternative energy sources in this country, $100 goes to the fossil fuel sector. It is already one of the most profitable industrial sectors on the face of the earth and the one most likely to bring the planet to its knees and to bring about the end of our own species, yet we continue to flagrantly fly in the face of the best scientific information available.
Let us take a look at some of the attempts by this government to move on sustainable development. I think, Madam Speaker, you would agree and any fair-minded Canadian would agree that not only has it been a fiscal failure but the will in cabinet has never been there to sustain it in terms of policy, financing or providing the personnel to do it. It was only a couple of months ago that the Minister of the Environment even got to chair the environment committee of cabinet. Until very recently it was chaired by another member of cabinet. The Minister of the Environment was not even able to make decisions in cabinet on major issues affecting the most important issue in the country.
Of the $3 billion that has been promised in terms of the green plan, as of this moment as we speak only $500 million has been spent to date. That was from $6 billion promised by the former Conservative minister who is now the leader of the Bloc Quebecois to $500 million, and that is after three years. The green plan on page 19 says and I quote: "As recommended in the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, the government now conducts environmental assessments of all proposed program and policy initiatives". That is a false statement and we know it.
May 13, 1993

What about the fixed link? Let us just spend a moment on that. The fixed link had a panel review and the generic concept was turned down. The panel unanimously said no. The Minister of Public Works gathered together friendly ice experts. I use the word experts advisedly since they never ever publish their results and never had their conclusions peer reviewed.
Now we have SCI, Strait Crossing Inc., the same group from Calgary that was involved in the Oldman River dam, with the same panel recommendations that have sat there for more than a year: 23 out of the 24. The number one recommendation was to tear down the Oldman River dam. It was so fiscally, economically and environmentally unsound that the panel recommended it should be torn down. The government said: "No, we will accept the other 23 recommendations and we will implement them". Neither the Minister of the Environment nor the Minister of Transport who were both responsible has ever implemented a single one of the mitigated recommendations. It is an insult to the intelligence of every Albertan and every Canadian no matter where they stand on the issue. It was a giant government fraud and Canadians are sickened by it.
On the fixed link, the Minister of Public Works plans to hand over $1.5 billion of our tax dollars on a bridge concept that has already been turned down by a public panel and public review.
There are entirely fraudulent hearings in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick and a 400-page document that most groups cannot get. They still do not have it. There is a press conference going on downstairs as we speak. They are trying to get some kind of sensible response out of the Government of Canada about the fixed link.
What about Bill C-13? We had to rush it through committee, sit late nights and hear witnesses long into the night. The minister appeared and said we had to rush, rush. We had to get the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act through that we could replace the 1984 cabinet guidelines order to bring certainty to the businesses of Canada. There was $15 billion in projects just waiting for the certainty of the new act.
The minister still has not taken the law list or any of the other lists to cabinet. We know he is busy running for the leadership but a piece of legislation so absolutely
Supply
fundamental to Canada's environment and economy is just sitting gathering dust.
With regard to the law list statutes are being pulled out by the dozens as we speak because of special deals being cut with industry. Special deals are being cut to remove statute after statute after statute. Those are the statutes that would automatically trigger an environmental assessment and a panel review. This government in order to curry favour with all its industrial contributors for elections campaigns is out there gutting a critical piece of legislation.
What about Kemano in my province? It was exempted by cabinet order. There are Liberal members on a joint committee of this House, the Standing Committee on Statutory Instruments and Regulations, who are sitting on it because they have discovered and agreed it is unconstitutional.
The minister who is running to be the Prime Minister of Canada and his cabinet colleagues unconstitutionally exempted Alcan. I wonder how large Alcan's contributions will be. I wonder how large SCI's contributions to the Conservatives will be over the next 35 years for the fixed link. At $42 million a year I would not be surprised if the words pay-off and kickback came pretty quickly to the minds of many Canadians about these kinds of projects.
The past should be our guide.

My friend from Vancouver Island reminds me historically how many times there have been these kinds of pay-offs in my own constituency. There have been many.
Let us take a look at more of the rhetoric for a moment. I want to give Canadians an opportunity to look at the rhetoric. The promises that have been made fiscally obviously were not made ingenuously. They were disingenuous. They were false and I suspect they were known to be false at the time they were made.
We find no other single fiscal category administered by the Conservative Government of Canada that has gone through such gigantic cuts since they were announced. None.
It can find $6 billion for helicopters that Canada does not need. We could remotor and re-equip our Labradors. We could remotor and re-equip our other aircraft in this country. That is what the American army did. It went to Boeing and it remotored. For $200 million we

May 13, 1993
Supply
could do the same thing in Canada but no, we need to have $6 billion worth of those helicopters.
Was there ever an environmental assessment done on that? No. Was there ever one done of the FTA? No. Was there ever a panel review done of NAFTA? No. They say we had a review. There is as much of an accurate review on the back of a box of Sugar Pops as there was of NAFTA.
The government likes to molly-coddle and twiddle and twaddle and force feed the Canadian public a whole lot of horse buns. The public is getting very sick of it. Canadians two to one now rate members of Parliament below convicted sex killers. It is because the benches of this place are loaded with people who not only go out and bluster with rhetoric; they lie to the public. They just lie to the public.
The government says it has a green plan and is going to clean up the Great Lakes. Our own Prime Minister signed an agreement for zero tolerance, for zero discharge into the Great Lakes with President Reagan in 1987 and then did nothing. The first major, measurable clean-up came as a result of Bob Rae's decision to move on the allowable levels of dioxins, furans and organo-chlorides going into Great Lakes water bodies.
Check with the IJC. The $25 million referred to in the green plan has done diddley squat in terms of a really serious clean-up on the Great Lakes. We have seen smoke and mirrors ad nauseam.
My friend from Davenport raised the issue of water export legislation. The Minister for International Trade and others are always rising from the bench and saying they have a policy that says no to major water exports from Canada.
The green plan in 1991 promised a safe water drinking act and a piece of legislation to ban major water exports from Canada. Was it rhetoric or was it a lie? I will let the Canadian public decide because neither has ever had first reading in this House. It is just smoke and mirrors.
Let us not forget what Simon Reisman and other negotiators had to say during the FTA. They said that water is what it is all about. I regret to say-
That is it.

I hear my friend from Broadview saying "that is it" and he is right. However I regret to say his own party during this Parliament voted on the floor of this House in favour of both the FTA, the member for Vancouver Quadra's fight of his life, and NAFTA.
Thirty-eight missing.
The Liberals voted for them both.
That's not true.

They do not even want to believe it themselves on the floor of the House. They should talk to their leader. I understand they were run in here to vote for the FTA and to vote for NAFTA to keep their corporate donations rolling in.
The Liberals brought this resolution to the floor today, but let us take a look at the simplistic press releases that continue to pour from their benches on highly complex issues. I must say I do not refer in this case to my friend from Davenport who has always been very thoughtful about his approach.
I raise one issue with the member for Ottawa West who blithely today, without even flinching, rose in this House and said it was the official policy of the Liberal Party of Canada if it was elected to add all of Clayoquot Sound to Pacific Rim National Park. She said it was the position of the member for LaSalle-Emard, herself, and the Liberal Party that if it became the government it would implement it.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have always had an enormous amount of respect for the member for Skeena, but he referred to people lying and putting forth facts in an untruthful way on the floor of the House. He suggested with his rhetoric that we in the Liberal Party supported the free trade agreement and NAFTA. He knows that is categorically false. If he wants to call somebody a liar, and by his words he is implicating all members of the Liberal Party, I think in fairness he should substantiate that, and I know he cannot substantiate that because it is not a true statement.

speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member actually called anyone a liar. I would have certainly asked him to withdraw. There seems to be a dispute here as to facts and this is not really a point of order.

Madam Speaker, it is unfortunate that the member for Skeena had such a lengthy outburst and reply. It did not allow the member from Broadview to make an inquiry which would not have been of political mischief in nature. It would have brought to his attention some of the recent misdeeds on the part of the Ontario government in the field of the environment.
In doing so perhaps we would have repaid in kind, but we would not have added very much to the debate because there is a limit to how much can be achieved in this Chamber by pointing at various provincial governments and their shortcomings in any specific policy field. When we engage in that we can have a great time. We can certainly score a lot of political points, but I do not know whether we would advance the discussion and merits of the measure we are debating here today.
Let me remind our listeners that we are debating today a motion by the Official Opposition, and more precisely by the member for Ottawa West, that expresses:
That this House regrets that, despite many grand announcements in international forums and despite the passage of two and one-half years since the launching of the green plan, the government has failed to integrate fully environmentally sustainable development as a goal of public policy.
This is the motion for debate and we are by virtue of this motion addressing the federal jurisdiction.
Because the concept is very well expressed, this motion also brings out the fact that this government has a big problem. It has a problem optically as well as intellectually. It can be boiled down into very simple terms. It sees the deficit in isolation and has an economic policy that is one dimensional with this enormous concern with inflation and deficit. This causes enormous problems in other fields, particularly unemployment and economic growth. It also has this habit and fixation of seeing business as the only partner in society, as if labour does not exist. The public interest includes business and labour and all those Canadians who do not see themselves as business or labour. Only the government can put forward a policy in the interest of the whole population.

In this kind of optical handicap with the deficit in isolation and business as the only partner it also tends to see despite the declaration that the environment is in isolation of the economy. That is the root of the problems we are attempting to discuss today.
We then have to analyse the reasons for this inability to look at society as a whole, the total economy and the total environment, which is more than just hugging trees or protecting bears. The environment is really all about ensuring that the base of our economy is sound and healthy. It is the foundation on which economies are built.
If the government fails to see the foundation and only sees the economy in isolation, sooner or later it is going to be in trouble because it overlooks its resources such as water, the atmosphere, the fisheries and so on. Sooner or later it is going to pay an enormous price which is sometimes straddled and stretched over several generations.
This government is extremely vulnerable on the question of water policy. We had a brief exchange with the parliamentary secretary on that. In 1991 the federal government will introduce a drinking water

We need a policy that will protect Canada from the demands of other jurisdictions and will ensure that quality is maintained and possibly improved. As a result of poor waste management some of our ground waters and water resources have been and continue to be

What is surprising and disturbing in this whole debate is that little attention has been given in recent times to a pattern of decisions by the government that has reversed virtually every recommendation made by environmental impact assessment panels.
As we know, we do establish panels when we have difficult and thorny environmental economic questions. We had that with the Rafferty-Alameda diversion proposal, the Oldman River dam, the Pearson runways, the Kemano dam project and the Prince Edward Island bridge link. We have done it with every thorny and difficult question. In every instance we have witnessed the government reversal of the recommendation made by the panel.

When it becomes a pattern and a consistent repetition of putting aside and reversing the recommendations by an environmental assessment panel, we begin to wonder whether the government is really serious when it says such great things in fora abroad or in Canada about the environment and sustainable development. In other words, the credibility of the government is seriously at stake.
Let me move beyond the environmental impact assessment because it is a bit of an unknown field and an evolving one. However it is a very important field, I must stress, and will be of increasing importance in the years

to come. It is just now beginning to appear on the Canadian political scene.
I will express another preoccupation and it is the following one. The government says in the green plan that it is really concerned with providing a framework of sustainable development for Canadians. In essence this means ensuring that we have environmentally sound economic growth. That is one way of putting it. Environmentally sound economic growth is in essence sustainable development. In other words, it will be sound in a manner that will ensure for the younger generation and their descendants the same access to opportunities and the quality of life we have enjoyed so far.
It is not closing options through misbehaviour and neglect but actually maintaining the options and possibly opening new options by treating our surrounding natural resources in a manner that will make them available in terms of our spiritual enjoyment, economic exploitation and the like to future generations of our species.
Canada has proclaimed its adherence and has embraced sustainable development since 1987 when the Brundtland report Our Common Future was made public. Since then it has failed to examine the way it spends money, sets up its taxation system, provides incentives and sets up programs under the auspices of the government and in the name of society at large. When we look at the yearly budgets since 1987 we find that year after year the Government of Canada spends billions and billions of dollars in providing subsidies, accelerated write-offs, incentives and programs which run counter to sustainable development.
Actually billions and billions of monetary resources that we have throughout the fiscal system are put behind unsustainable activities. These unsustainable activities ought to be instead the top priority of the Government of Canada. There is no doubt in my mind. In particular we find them more easily identifiable when we analyse the budget and the fiscal measures made available to the energy sector. As we all know it is the production of energy, transportation, trade and other human activities, but particularly the production of energy that causes pollution and endangers and accelerates the process of climate warming.

Madam Speaker, I too want to say a few words in connection with this opposition motion. As all opposition motions traditionally do, it condemns the government for the differences between what it says in connection with the green plan and what it has been doing since the green plan went into effect some two and a half years ago.
I am particularly pleased to have this opportunity to speak in connection with this motion and the green plan because apart from the economy the environment is perhaps the number one priority of Canadians in my own constituency and right across this land.
I had the privilege of being in cabinet at the time the green plan was developed. I was certainly privy to many of the discussions and debates in connection to working out the concept of the green plan and putting it in place.
The green plan as you know, Madam Speaker, and as I hope Canadians are aware is a very major initiative. It is perhaps not unique but it is one of the very few initiatives of this sort that has been undertaken by any country anywhere in the world. People such as former Prime Minister Brundtland of Norway who headed the Brundtland commission have commented on the fact that Canada has taken a very major lead in the world in environmental matters. She did not say that just because we have been putting forth words. She said that because we have been putting deeds behind those words.
The aim of the green plan when it was put into effect was to make our country the world's most environmentally friendly nation by the year 2000. The program was to be phased over a period of years. It was to set goals, targets and schedules for policies and programs that deal with our land, water and air; our problems with waste and energy efficiency; our agriculture, forests, fisheries, parks and wildlife; the vast northern reaches of this country; environmental emergencies; local issues such as tree planting; waste reduction, global warming and the Great Lakes pollution.
The plan has a tremendous scope and was to take effect over a period of years but not just a finite and terminable period of years. It was not and is not intended to come to an end after five or six years. It has been

The whole process and the problem we have with our environment did not just develop overnight. It did not happen as a result of one enormous act or one enormous impact from one source. It has come about as a result of a great many micro actions, not only on the part of government but on the part of all Canadians.

It is not going to come by making some pronouncement or by taking one individual action on the part of government. It is an effort that has to be made individually and in an enormous number of ways by government, business and each and every Canadian personally in their homes and in their own personal lives.
Today the Minister of the Environment, who I have an enormous amount of personal respect for, has asked me to deal with one aspect of the green plan and the actions we have put behind our words in the green plan. That aspect relates to energy and sustainable development with respect to energy.
As the members of this House and Canadians I trust are aware there is a fundamental conflict between the whole concept of dealing with sustainable development, dealing with the environment problems and the energy sector. Environmental concerns traditionally have not been the major focus of the energy sector.
When we start to focus on energy and sustainable development, it takes a considerable amount of readjustment and refocusing. However it is vitally important. I believe that everyone connected with the energy sector recognizes that fact now. It is vitally important, particularly in the area of global warming, what is happening to our country and to our earth in that regard.
The subject of energy and sustainable development is very complex. It involves social, economic, technological and environmental factors. In spite of the complexity of
the problem sustainable development, since the green plan has been put into effect, has become a fundamental part of Canada's energy policy.
The integration of environmental and economic goals of all Canadians is a major priority of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources that is known to us in Ottawa as EMR. That has happened because of the green plan.
My own personal opinion is that without the green plan it is very unlikely that there would have been this change of focus and the integration of environmental and economic goals as a major priority of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. EMR was, as I am well aware having been in cabinet at that time, very much involved in the preparation of the green plan which is as indicated based on the principles of sustainable development.
As a result a number of specific initiatives relating to energy are outlined in the green plan. The details of these have been announced from time to time by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Most of these initiatives are designed to promote energy efficiency and conservation. The government believes that energy efficiency is the best way to begin to address many of the environmental problems associated with energy production, its use and particularly with global warming.
The green plan contains a commitment to help reduce barriers to alternative and renewable energy sources in Canada. These measures increase the options available to maximize efficiency and minimize the environmental impacts of energy production and use.
The green plan was introduced some two and a half years ago. By the first anniversary of the green plan a year and a half ago, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources introduced in this House as part of the energy efficiency and alternative energy program of the Government of Canada a new Energy Efficiency Act.
This act represents one step in the implementation of a broadly based program involving all types of fuels and energy using sectors of the Canadian economy. It uses targeted information programs, persuasion, regulation and research development.

More specifically that act provides for minimum energy efficiency standards to phase out inefficient energy using equipment and household appliances. It also has an Energuide labelling program to provide consumers with better information about energy use by major household appliances. Included as well is a national energy use data base on energy consumption and the use of alternative energy in our country.
You will recall that the Energy Efficiency Act was passed by both this House and by the Senate and received royal assent in June 1992. It came into force at the beginning of this year.
In addition to that act, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources also announced before the first anniversary of the green plan a series of initiatives that were aimed at improving energy efficiency in buildings in Canada. That is something that is of great concern to me and was of great concern to me in my former role as the minister of housing.
These particular initiatives which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources introduced include a building energy code to develop national energy codes and specific minimum acceptable performance levels, a code which the government intends to promote and do its best to see incorporated into provincial and municipal building codes.
That is not always an easy matter. We, as the Government of Canada, have certain constitutional jurisdictional powers and we can develop a code of this sort, but it is not as easy as just snapping our fingers or passing a law or trying to impose these codes on other jurisdictions. The provinces have a separate jurisdiction under the Constitution and the municipalities are creatures of the provinces so they are governed by that provincial jurisdiction as well. While we can set these codes it is not as easy as it might seem to actually put them in place. We have to use efforts of persuasion and leadership to get other levels of government to implement these codes in order to make them work.
Therefore it is one thing for opposition members to condemn the government for not having these put in place yet but it is another thing from a practical sense to accomplish that goal.

Obviously we want to promote energy efficiency but at the same time there is a cost involved that has to be taken into account. It is an upfront cost. Whereas if they were looking at the longer term and they had the wherewithal to do it, they could afford to buy it. There would be savings down the road but those savings are not up front. It is easier said than done, particularly when in a leadership role we are trying to convince the provinces and the private sector to introduce this kind of a program.
