There is something called the smart house which you may or may not be familiar with, Madam Speaker, but that is another effort at producing energy efficiency in housing. More and more we are going to see this sort of thing in new housing, but again the whole issue of the initial affordability is one of the major deterrents that has to be dealt with in order to get this kind of program into effect.
In addition, by the first anniversary of the green plan the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had also introduced the buildings research and development and technology transfer program, the Canada Centre for Mineral and Energy Technology, CANMET. That was

May 13, 1993

put in place to develop and commercialise energy efficient and passive solar technologies in residential and commercial sectors.
Again there are problems of upfront costs with all of these things which means that they are not universally adopted or embraced by the private sector and by Canadians as a whole. CANMET itself has been a world leader in developing environmentally responsible approaches to producing and to using energy resources.
Then, as well, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has announced the federal buildings initiative. That is a program designed to help improve energy efficiency in all the federal department buildings and facilities. As we know the federal buildings initiative falls under the environmental stewardship program in which the federal government is trying to lead by example in demonstrating its firm commitment to the principle of sustainable development.
The greening of Parliament Hill program was announced just over a year ago. It is another part of this and it is aimed at introducing more energy efficient lighting on Parliament Hill. It is, as you and I, Madam Speaker, all members of Parliament and everyone who works on Parliament Hill know, a good example of the commitment of the government to putting its own house in order. Quite clearly, it is important for the government to show leadership. If it is going to be advocating sustainable development by all Canadians, the government itself is going to have to demonstrate that it is prepared to do it itself. The greening of the Hill program is one way in which the government is putting that forward.
Obviously the Speaker has had a major role in the whole program. I want to compliment you, Madam Speaker, for the role you have played in putting that into effect as well. That is a true leadership role.
Finally, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has announced a series of initiatives designed to improve the performance and expand the availability and use of alternative transportation fuels through technology, market development programs and research and development into such alternatives as natural gas, propane, alcohol fuels and electric powered vehicles.
All of those things are positive steps that were done by the first anniversary of the announcement of the green plan. Those positive things were done by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the minister and the government in conjunction with the green plan. Therefore when it is alleged that nothing has happened and that no steps have been taken, then quite clearly a considerable number of initiatives were undertaken and put forth by the first anniversary of this plan and more have been undertaken since the first anniversary of the green plan.
When the second anniversary of the green plan arrived, and that was last December as we will recall, many of the Energy, Mines and Resources programs referred to were well under way. There were several new ones that had been announced as well. The government, however, cannot act alone. It has to work with the provinces and the private sector if we are going to make some meaningful progress toward achieving both economic and environmental goals. Last September, Energy, Mines and Resources released a discussion paper on efficiency regulations and equipment labelling as the basis for public consultations throughout Canada. That was the first step in an open and constructive dialogue with the provinces and territorial governments.
I notice my time has expired. I have a lot more to say, as Your Honour can appreciate because there were a lot of other initiatives undertaken by Energy, Mines and Resources. They were veiy positive things that were very contrary to the allegations of the opposition. Perhaps I will have an opportunity to comment on some of those during comments and questions period.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a short statement before I ask the hon. member for Don Valley East to respond.
I would like to refer to two particular budgets that this government has brought down. One was in 1989 when the government, without warning to the province, to the town of Summerside or to anyone, announced the closure of Canadian Forces Base Summerside. I know the member was a member of the cabinet at that time and I think he was one of the few members who did visit

May 13, 1993
Supply
the town to see what the impact of that particular budget measure was.
Four years later, in the May budget of this year, the government made an announcement which pretty well blind sided the province, the Government of P.E.I. and the forest industry of P.E.I. when it announced that it would no longer be funding ERDAs.
I would like to quote from a letter to the minister responsible for ACOA, the hon. member for St. John's West, from Ian Dennison who is the president of the Forest Industry Association of Prince Edward Island. Mr. Dennison said that one sentence from the federal budget has effectively devastated an entire industry in Prince Edward Island and it reads like this: "The government will not be reviewing the present federal-provincial agreement on economic and regional development in forestry and minerals, recognizing that these are essentially geared to areas of provincial jurisdiction and ones where provincial governments and private sector activities have matured to the point where more limited federal government involvement is warranted".
That was the line which pretty well destroyed 10 years of development in the forest industry in P.E.I. The 10 years of development and investment by the public sector and the private sector is just gone overnight. They have had 10 years of developing expertise, people have had training, they have gone to schools and universities to acquire expertise in the silviculture area and in reforestation. The whole effort is wasted.
What a tragedy.

Why is just Prince Edward Island affected here? Prince Edward Island is affected because our federal-provincial agreements in forestry expired last March and the federal government knew our agreements had expired last March. Seven provinces have at least two years to go in their agreements. This will give them some cushion so they can soften the impact and make conditional plans. Quebec has had three years to plan for the changes proposed in the budget. I think New Brunswick has one year. Prince Edward Island had absolutely no time to adjust to the new conditions that today are a reality.
It did not hint to Prince Edward Island that these changes were coming. The federal government knew that our forestry agreement was going to expire. In
negotiations with the federal government, they were discussing another five-year plan. On March 1,1 believe ACOA then switched roles and said: "We would like to discuss a one-year extension. We would like to evaluate what has gone on in the past five years so we are going to propose a one-year extension". Then the budget came along and there was nothing.
Overtures have been made to both ministers responsible for ACOA and the forestry minister for an extension. We are requesting an extension so that the blow will be softened somewhat. To this point much like the CFB discussions at the time it was like hitting a dead wall.
In 1989 the community in P.E.I. rallied around to support the town and the people affected by the closure of the base. As stated in the recent edition of The Guardian, Alex Campbell, a contractor and owner of JAC Forestry Products in the Belfast area said: "It is easy for government to stop funding the forest because so few people can see the value. We do not make enough noise I guess. The general public should wake up and take notice. It would be the environment that takes this on the chin".
I would like the hon. member to comment on what sense it makes for government to do this, at this time and in this particular way.
The environment is uppermost in people's minds. The government is proposing the green plan. It attended the Rio conference. At the same time there seems to have been no planning, forethought or any concern for the people employed in the forestry industry on Prince Edward Island nor for any other province which in the future cannot afford to come into these programs on its own because it just does not have the resources to fix up 200 years of neglect in a 10-year period. All of sudden they are left on their own and unfunded. Basically the government is saying it is not really concerned: "You are on your own. We have made the decision. Goodbye forestry industry in Prince Edward Island".
I would like the member to respond to that and to bring these concerns to his caucus and government about the state of affairs in the forestry industry in Prince Edward Island.

I understand fully the concerns put forward by the member from Prince Edward Island.

As he indicated, at the time of the base closure in Summerside I certainly did visit Prince Edward Island. I had visited P.E.I. before the base closure and I visited after.
I had numerous discussions with residents including the mayor of Summerside. The hon. member knows the mayor of Summerside very well. I had a number of discussions with him relating to the problem and the adjustment problem.
As the member is aware, a form of adjustment was put in place by the government with the location of the GST operation in Summerside. The government was certainly not insensitive to the problems encountered in Summer-side. Although it did not happen overnight an effort was made at providing an adjustment program and that was done.
With respect to the forestry situation, it could very well be there might be some further adjustment program. I suspect in the circumstances as the hon. member has indicated the government certainly would be prepared to listen.
In my view this is not a hard-hearted, hard-nosed, insensitive government. With respect to Summerside, it listened to the concerns and acted on them. It has done the same in other cases as well. I point out the case of municipal grants in lieu. There was a freeze announced on that and there had been adjustments made in that. This government does take into account particular adjustment problems and I am sure it will look at that very carefully.
The hon. member has to recognize two other things however and I know he does. I know he recognizes we have enormous deficit and debt problem. He and his party recognize that fact and want to address it. The difficulty is how to address it. How do we address it fairly and in the best way? Everybody has their own views on that. However, when it affects us or our constituents personally, obviously we are inclined to object strenuously and say that spending should be cut in some other area or on some other person, but it should not be done to us. That is natural and understandable, but unfortunately we seem to have come to the point where that is an impossibility. Everybody is going to have to be affected in some way by these things.
The other thing I would just remind the hon. member is something called the Charlottetown accord. Under the provisions of the Charlottetown accord which I believe the hon. member supported although I know his seat-mate had some reservations-
I did not support it.

No, you are not the hon. member to whom I was referring. I was referring to the hon. member from Prince Edward Island. I believe he supported the Charlottetown accord. I know the premier of his province supported the Charlottetown accord.
Under that provision forestry was to become a provincial jurisdiction. The province of Prince Edward Island, the government of the province of Prince Edward Island and the present government of Prince Edward Island were supporters of the principle that forestry was to become a provincial jurisdiction.
In fact, although the people of Canada did not favour the entire accord and voted against it, at the same time that principle was certainly supported by all of the provincial governments. All of the provincial premiers agreed with the provision of the accord, that forestry would become a provincial matter.
I suggest to the hon. member that while there is certainly an adjustment problem here, it is a situation that was accepted and agreed to by the government of his own province and by the hon. member himself.

Mr. Speaker, this is National Police Week in Canada. I wish to take this occasion to extend to police forces across our country the appreciation of this House and all Canadians for the service they provide to the public.
In addition to their regular duties, police forces throughout Canada undertake various charitable and community-related activities. One of these is the law enforcement torch run on behalf of the Special Olympics.
Sponsored by the Association of Chiefs of Police, the torch run is in its seventh year. The money collected from the run is donated to the Special Olympics for the benefit of the developmentally challenged. This year over 12,000 runners hope to raise $2 million for this worth-while cause.
The torch run for the Special Olympics is another example of how Canada's law enforcement officers go above and beyond the call of duty in the service and protection of our communities.

Mr. Speaker, one year ago the subcommittee on health issues submitted a report on foetal alcohol syndrome. The government has acted quickly on some of the recommendations but has not acted on others, particularly the request for the labelling of all alcoholic products sold in Canada.
This week the American Paediatric Society released a statement that women should completely abstain from the use of alcohol during pregnancy. This fact is coupled with the report from the U.S. Centre for Disease Control and Prevention that the number of foetal alcohol syndrome babies has tripled since 1979, largely due to better recognition and reporting.
In light of this information, I would request that the government reconsider its position and proceed with the appropriate labelling of all alcohol-containing products
sold in Canada with a format similar to that used on tobacco products.

Mr. Speaker, the government will have to take a position soon on the future of air transport in Canada.
If the government goes along with the agreement between PWA and American Airlines, not only PWAbut eventually Air Canada will be taken over by American companies. Such a resolution of the present crisis would lead in the short term to the disappearance of the Canadian air transport industry.
This would also lead to major job losses in Montreal, which is already hard hit by unemployment.
The only solution is for Air Canada and PWA to merge and for this government to abandon its absurd utopian policy of deregulation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the House a notice that was sent on May 8, 1993 by the Minister of National Revenue to all fishermen in the gulf region of Newfoundland and Labrador. It said that the excise tax rebate of four cents a litre, which has been in place for the last 20 to 25 years, has been withdrawn effective May 8.
This regulation is discriminatory because it would only apply to fishermen who live along the gulf coast of Newfoundland, Quebec, Nova Scotia, P.E.I. or New Brunswick. All fishermen in Atlantic Canada who live along the Atlantic coast will continue to receive this four cent a litre rebate from the Government of Canada.
The effect of this discriminatory and ill-conceived new policy will be to make fishermen in the gulf zone, and I know the Speaker as a former minister of fisheries will appreciate this, non-competitive with their counterparts elsewhere in the region. It is without rationale. It cannot be squared away on the basis of fairness.

May 13, 1993
I ask the government to come to its senses and please withdraw this discriminatory action by the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is a sad day for the people of the Quebec City area.
This morning we learned that at dawn today, May 13, 1993, a priceless jewel of our heritage, Montmorency Manor, was ravaged by flames.
This manor contained major items from our history and was our pride. It was also a leading tourist attraction and for several months had been undergoing renovation to make it more welcoming and comfortable for visitors from all parts of the world.
Being born and raised in Cote-de-Beaupre, I feel particularly touched by this sad event. I hope it will be possible to recreate this symbol in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, I call to the attention of the House the terrible decision by Bob Rae's NDP government in Toronto to close the New Liskeard Agriculture College.
This college has trained thousands of young people for over 70 years to be good farmers, good scientists and technicians and good citizens. It has provided a centre for continuing education and extension work for rural communities throughout the north.
It is the centre for agriculture research in northern Ontario with important laboratories for animal health. It is the centre for equine research and development for eastern Canada. It is essential to the future development of agriculture in Ontario and to the economy of the tri-town area.
I am sure that every member of this House, including NDP MPs, join me in condemning this move by Bob Rae and his government and call upon him to reverse it and do it immediately.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Seniors); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in May 1993, the Department of National Health and Welfare launched the third edition of the catalogue of audio-visuals on family violence. This detailed catalogue lists more than 850 films and videos produced in North America which deal with issues related to family violence, including child abuse and neglect, sexual abuse of children, marital violence and mistreatment of the elderly.
The catalogue of audio-visuals on family violence fully reflects the cooperation between the National Film Board and the Department of National Health and Welfare which has been going on since 1978. More than 8.5 million people have seen a film on family violence since the first edition was published.
Professionals, front-line workers, researchers, educators and community groups use films and videos to raise public awareness, for professional training and for education. The Department of National Health and Welfare is proud to cooperate with the National Film Board and firmly believes that the catalogue will help communities and Canadians prevent violence.

Mr. Speaker, the last Conservative budget shows that poor people and off-reserve natives cannot rely on this government to help break the poverty cycle.
Since 1991 this government has cut 61 per cent from the budgets of the Rural and Native Housing Program and the Urban Native Housing Program.
The budget for CMHC was frozen by the Conservatives and as a result funding for the Rural and Native Housing Program, the Urban Native Housing Program and the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program will not be renewed.
May 13, 1993

These programs helped to ensure that people with limited income could afford safe and adequate housing while allowing them to use their money to help stop the cycle of poverty.
In these days of high unemployment brought about by the failed economic policies of the Liberals and the Conservatives, more people than ever need help finding adequate housing. If this government cared about Canadians it would not have cut back funding for these veiy necessary programs.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to share with the House more of the opinions expressed by residents of Edmonton- Strathcona in my recent survey of the riding.
I asked my constituents what they would do about the GST. If we were to believe the voices of the opposition and certain interest groups, Canadians are furious about the GST and want it abolished.
My constituents tell me otherwise. In fact, a strong majority of the survey respondents said that they would like to keep the GST as long as its revenues are dedicated to deficit reduction. Less than 20 per cent of the respondents want to see the GST abolished. GST revenues are going toward deficit reduction through the Debt Servicing and Reduction Account.
In my view, this survey result does not indicate that my constituents are happy about the GST but it clearly shows that they are aware of the debt crisis and the importance of the revenues collected by the GST. In other words, we may not like the taste of the medicine but we know enough to take it when we are sick.
Canadians know that tough measures are required to address our deficit situation and they support the bold steps taken by our government to get our fiscal house in order.

Mr. Speaker, while the Prime Minister traipses around the world at taxpayers' expense I can only hope that he has not lost
sight of the many important issues that are on the minds of Canadians today.
As the Prime Minister meets with world leaders he has given himself the ideal opportunity to advance Canada's interests on a wide variety of issues. Canadians are concerned that they have heard nothing from the Prime Minister regarding this government's commitment to resolve outstanding trade problems. The Prime Minister should be taking advantage of this international stage to lobby hard on behalf of our supply-managed farmers for a strengthened article XI at the GATT.
This farewell tour is costing Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars. As the Prime Minister jet-sets back to Canada, Canadians can only hope that Canada is getting something out of all of this, something for our money. Canadians expect that while the Prime Minister is abroad he is working in the best interest of this country, not just in the best interest of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, today the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans took an important step toward reforming the licensing allocation and sanction systems of Canada's fisheries. Until now the minister had absolute discretion over licensing and allocation. The legislation tabled today in the House will create two independent fisheries boards for each of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. These boards will license fishermen and allocate the annual harvest as well as applying sanctions for fisheries violations by commercial licence holders.
This legislation will allow those directly involved in the fishing industry a degree of input into the decision-making process that affects their lives.
It is for this reason that I commend the minister for taking the initiative to launch these reforms.

Mr. Speaker, Saturday, as many members of this House return to their ridings for the next week, thousands and thousands of Canadians will be arriving in Ottawa to reclaim our future and protest the failed Liberal and Conservative

May 13, 1993
policies over the last decade, policies which benefit corporations and the wealthy.
All across Canada buses, trains, planes and car pools are now being organized. Working people in every province and territory are getting together for this giant rally to say no to the free trade agreement, no to NAFTA, no to the GST, no to health care cuts, no to education cuts and no to public sector worker bashing.
Even the municipal council of Ottawa, not known for its left-leaning views, has declared Saturday, May 15 people's agenda day. Those who are fed up will show up and more than tulips will be showing on Parliament Hill.
So to my colleagues in this House, as you head for home, know that those at home are heading for Ottawa to tell you just what they think of your failed Liberal and Conservative policies. They will be here to reclaim their future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate Paul Blanchard and Kevin Mathews of Canada Composting who have embarked on a $20 million pilot project to build and demonstrate a large-scale centralized waste conversion facility in Newmarket, Ontario.
With the support of Environment Canada through the D-Rect program, Demonstration of Resource and Energy Conservation Technology, and joint venture capital investments from the private sector this project is expected to be accepting customer waste next year. This plant will have the capacity to process 75,000 tonnes of waste annually, recycling 80 per cent of this for compost, for nurseries, landscapers and the general public for home garden use.
This brand new technology and new procedure has the potential of being very helpful in meeting Canada's green plan target of a 50 per cent reduction in the amount of waste going to landfills by the year 2000.
Congratulations to Canada Composting, the town of Newmarket and the federal Minister of the Environment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the majority in this country that there are still very deep needs in the minority groups. I want to remind the majority in this country that anybody living west of Ontario who speaks French does not have access to a post-secondary institution.
I want to remind the people of this country that every French-speaking minority living west of Ontario does not have control of its schools. I want to remind Ontario that there are negotiations.
Yesterday, the minister-and I see her in the House-reminded us, and I quote from page 19316 from Hansard:
My proposals are on the table, my budgets are ready, and it is now
up to the Ontario government to go ahead with the discussions.
I implore this government to get with it and ask Ontario to come to the table and settle that document concerning the future of this country and give our kids their education.

Mr. Speaker, the first week of June is National Access Awareness Week. Teams of politicians, disabled individuals, labour leaders, people from the business community and from all walks of life have been busy throughout the year in efforts to eliminate barriers facing persons with disabilities.
Canada's Secretary of State and minister responsible for the status of disabled persons has taken our experiences on disability to the world stage. Together with international colleagues and leaders from the disability community, she has pioneered an initiative to improve the quality of life for the world's 500 million people who are disabled.
Mr. Speaker, we have appreciated your ongoing support of National Access Awareness Week and the concern you have for accessibility to all aspects of Parliament.
May 13, 1993

I want to urge all members of the House to support National Access Awareness Week in the communities throughout their ridings. We can build together on the minister's their your leadership and our record of achievement.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of fisheries released legislation today providing for a new regime in the fisheries, a new system of licensing, a new system of allocating the resource.
The one very good thing about the legislation is it provides lots of lead time. The minister said it would not come into effect, he expects, until January 1, 1995 and it is going to need that much time. It is a substantial change.
The minister has a better appreciation of the need to take time for things like this, having gone through the introduction of the aboriginal fish strategy on the west coast. Last year was a disaster. That is the only word I can use to describe it, although the minister would rather not use that word.
I am not sure this year is going to be that much better. We have had one indication already there could be problems when the Sto:lo decided to fish when they were not supposed to fish. The minister said that those who were fishing did not know they were transgressing, so nothing was done about it.
However, it is sending a signal that DFO is still not prepared to deal with people that break fishing regulations. If that is the way it is going to start, then we could be in trouble this fishing season in B.C.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to convey to the House that CFB Edmonton has recently founded its 18 Wing.
The Wing is an organizational structure patterned after the Royal Air Force and used in Canada until unification of the Canadian forces in 1968. It replaces the concept of a base. The Wing emphasizes the operational character, rather than the support function of Canadian
Oral Questions
air bases. Air Command has now created an organization that is more consistent with air force aims, missions and tasks.
I was pleased to be at the ceremony in April to celebrate the formation. Congratulations Colonel Mike Wansink and CFB Edmonton men and women serving their country in 18 Wing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
I want to join with the leader of the Liberal Party in praising the minister of health for supporting the basic principles of medicare.
The Liberal Party condemns the two front runners in the Conservative leadership race for their attack on medicare. In the first place it was incredible that they said they were in favour of user fees. It was unbelievable that they repeated they were open to the concept of user fees for sick Canadians after the minister of health made his statement yesterday.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if the government agrees with the position of the minister of health on this issue or does the government support the position of the two Tory leadership contenders?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday on television, the two Tory leadership contenders repeated that they were open to considering medicare user fees, even after the Minister of National Health and Welfare said: "not to follow that line, because it will destroy the health care system". Don't the two leadership contenders realize that in Canada health is a right, not a privilege? Could the Deputy Prime Minister tell us why the Tory leadership candidates want

May 13, 1993

to consider user fees that would undermine the universality of our health care system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my answer in French is the same as the answer I gave earlier in English. The position of the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare remains the same and is not expected to change in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, we know what the minister of health said and we support him.
The question we are asking the government is this. Why is it that the two chief candidates for the leadership of his party have ignored the advice of the Minister of National Health and Welfare? This is Canada, not the United States. We do not want to turn people away from the hospitals because they are poor.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister denounce his two cabinet colleagues, who are so desperate for right wing votes in the Tory party, they are prepared to sell out the sacred principles of universal medicare?
I have listened to the question and I do not think it has anything to do with the administration of government.

Mr. Speaker, since January 1989 Canada has lost 295,000 or 14 per cent of its manufacturing jobs.
Would the Acting Prime Minister tell us why his government is proud of this record?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is very well aware of the major restructuring that has taken place in the manufacturing sector, not only here in Canada but in the United States and other industrialized countries as well. Canada has gone through that process.
In the course of it, our productivity has been enhanced dramatically, our competitiveness has been improved,
and we are now seeing the benefits of that in the exports that are growing day by day, week by week and month by month.
While there are fewer numbers of people working in the manufacturing sector, the output is increasing very dramatically. I think if he were to go back to the 1950s he would see that probably 30 per cent of the Canadian labour force was employed in the manufacturing sector. Today it is probably 15 per cent or 16 per cent, yet the output has tripled in that period of time. That is a pretty good record for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if the Tory policies have been working so well over these past four years, why has Canada lost manufacturing jobs at twice the U.S. rate?
Why have 15,400 Canadian steel workers lost their jobs and 16,000 Canadian auto workers lost their jobs? Why has unemployment in Montreal gone from 9.5 per cent to 13.7 per cent? Why has the number of people in Toronto without a job more than tripled, going from 69,000 to 208,000?
Why will this government not come clean and admit that its legacy to Canada is lost jobs and lost hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason why a deeper adjustment has had to take place in Canada as compared to the United States-and the hon. member knows this very well-is that the labour input costs were much higher in Canada than they were in the United States and our productivity slipped.
It is a combination of enhanced productivity, retooling and utilizing the latest equipment. That is precisely why we took action in the February budget to improve the competitiveness, improve the tax environment. That is why in December we took action in the small business sector to improve the tax environment, to improve the environment for business to do business.
I am pleased to note that manufacturing employment is up 28,000, up 4 per cent in the last six months or 70,000 jobs. Surveys indicate that the manufacturing output is going to be increased by 33 per cent of those who have been surveyed. Ontario in the past year has picked up 63 per cent of the new jobs created in the country, and most of those were in the manufacturing sector.
May 13, 1993

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
There is probably no other program in Canada that Canadians are more proud of than our system of universal health care. Not only is it an important program for families, for people in every province and territory, but it is a fundamental part of our economic system.
In fact, the kind of system we have is a great asset to business because it is not a business expense. It is something we all share because we all believe that health care is very important and must be available to everyone.
People are getting a bit confused. We have, for example, the health minister warning yesterday that the introduction of user fees would "destroy the health care system" and would create "two health care systems, one for the privileged and another for the less fortunate".
Is it the policy of the Conservative Party and this Conservative government to end universality of health care and create a two-tiered system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the minister of health stated very clearly was that the five principles enshrined in the Canada Health Act, namely accessibility, universality, portability, comprehensiveness and public administration are all fundamental to the Canadian health care system.
The hon. member knows very well that all provinces and all governments are faced with increased health care costs. All governments have been trying to address the issue of cost containment.
She knows very well that the province of Saskatchewan has reduced funding for health care. As a matter of fact, I would suspect we may expect much the same kind of an approach in Ontario.
When we had an opportunity to meet with the federal and provincial health and finance ministers, we talked about these challenges in a very meaningful way. Clearly we cannot ignore the fact that we have to find ways and means to fund the health care system. But there is
Oral Questions
certainly no deviation from the five fundamental principles that are enshrined in the Canada Health Act.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary.
I can suggest some ways the government can find the funds. Close some of the tax loopholes for the rich and the privileged and put the funds into health care.
The federal government has reduced its share of health funding from 43 per cent in 1984 to 33 per cent today. If this pattern continues, by the year 2010 the federal government will be putting no funds into health care. In order to maintain the principles of the Canada Health Act the federal government has to have a role in funding health care if we want a national system.
I ask the Acting Prime Minister this. Clearly the government, the Conservative Party is trying to have it both ways. We have seen that with the Liberals. Some support user fees and some do not support user fees.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if his government, his party stands for universal health care. Will he commit today that the government will ensure there is a national health care system in this country that we can all be proud of without user fees?

It amounts to an excess of $40 billion and it continues to grow, not shrink, like the hon. member suggests.

What we are doing here is notwithstanding the fact that we are containing government expenditures at zero real growth, or roughly 1.5 per cent to 1.7 per cent. Federal transfers are growing at an annualized rate of just under 4 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the government House leader.
The high reputation of our Canadian Armed Forces is based in large part on its proud record of battle in the Second World War when it fought against those who bore the swastika flag and the acts of inhumanity and injustice associated with it.
Yesterday the minister was quoted as suggesting that a currently serving member of the Canadian Armed Forces who erected a swastika flag in a Canadian military barracks and then stood under it giving the Hitler salute and wearing a Nazi T-shirt was just engaging in a "boyish prank".
Why is the minister on behalf of the Conservative government allowing the reputation of our Canadian Armed Forces to be undermined by the way he and the Conservative government appear to be tolerating and making light of this kind of despicable conduct?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not say he was engaging; I said that I did not know what was happening.
The particular soldier in question said that it was just a stunt. He has also apparently said to his supervisors that he is no longer a member of the Heritage Front organization and no longer participates in that.
In any event the policies of the Canadian Armed Forces in respect of behaviour are quite clear. Any behaviour reflecting biases, prejudices, racism and so on that might be exhibited by any soldier is improper and grounds for dismissal from the Canadian Armed Forces. The whole question is being looked into.
All I suggested when I was being pressured during the scrum was that I have complete faith in the Canadian Armed Forces and the process in place. I do not believe that the leadership of the Canadian Armed Forces is any more tolerant of the kind of behaviour the hon. member talked about than he is.

Mr. Speaker, I am talking about what is tolerated by this Conservative government.
The minister may tiy to suggest that the conduct is not tolerated by the Conservative government. However, after the white supremacist neo-Nazi conduct of the individual in question became known, that individual was promoted and sent to serve in a non-white country.
I ask the minister why he and the Conservative government do not recognize that the way in which he and the government are talking about this situation is offensive to the vast majority of Canadians. For them, the conduct photographed in that Canadian military barracks is not only contrary to the proud reputation of our Canadian Armed Forces but totally inconsistent with and contraiy to our fundamental Canadian values.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):

Mr. Speaker, one of the values I am sure the hon. member shares

with everybody else in the House is our commitment to the charter of rights and all that implies in terms of freedoms. I hope the hon. member is not suggesting we would get a situation where at the political level, the ministerial level, decisions would be made affecting individual soldiers. I hope he recognizes the wisdom of policies being put in place by the political masters as they are against this kind of behaviour. The policies should be implemented by the professionals in the Canadian military. I have every confidence they will do so and do so properly.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister.

The member for Windsor West has pointed out to the minister that the Minister of National Defence has accepted the characterization of the activity in the Canadian forces barracks involving swastikas as youthful folly. The member for Windsor West has pointed out that this activity for reasons understood by all Canadians is extremely offensive to the many thousands who fought and served during the World War. Some made the ultimate sacrifice. It besmirches the reputation of a truly great and honourable organization, the Canadian Armed Forces.
What the member for Windsor West has asked for and what the minister is being asked to give is an apology to the people of Canada for making light of truly abhorrent behaviour.

Mr. Speaker, the minister still has not understood that we are talking about the competence and the appropriateness of the actions of ministers, not the Canadian Armed Forces.

member to think for half a minute that there is the possibility it was a prank.

The Conference Board has just reported that incomes in this country have dropped for the last three consecutive years. speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is why I have said in this House so many times and why we practise the fact that we should bring our deficit under control through spending cuts and expenditure reductions rather than through increased taxes. That is precisely what we did in the February budget and that is exactly what we did in the December statement and a number of those initiatives are starting to have effect.
For example, we talked about the improvement in the competitiveness and the productivity of the manufacturing sector as a result of a number of initiatives that we took. In the small business sector, there were a number of initiatives taken both in the February budget and in the December statement. There were a number of initiatives that were proposed with respect to infrastructure improvement, training, skills upgrading and initiatives with respect to the housing sector. All these things are now starting to take hold.
That is why we have had growth over the last three months, real GDP growth, of some 4 per cent. That was followed by a third quarter growth of 3.5 per cent. Jobs are being created. Business activity is starting to become more stimulated. Most important, what we are seeing is continued expansion in our exports, particularly exports to the United States, which has been a veiy positive indicator in our total economy.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has relied on growth in our economy by increased exports to the United States. Unfortunately the growth rate in the first quarter in the U.S. this year is down to 1.9 per cent compared to 4.8 per cent in the last quarter of 1992, so we may be in for some surprises very soon.
In light of that and in light of the fact that incomes have fallen in the last three years by about $1,200 a person or a drop of 5.5 per cent, I want to once again ask the minister: Why not declare a war on unemployment? Why not a jobs plan in this country where more money is put into creating long-term jobs in Canada? Why not do something like that and put people to work? That is the best way to bring down the deficit.
May 13, 1993

While I am on my feet I want to correct the record for the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle who asked me about the status of the artists. We proclaimed on Tuesday part I, not part II. I am not quite sure why. I will have to get back to him on the remainder. I apologize for any confusion that may have caused.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the minister this in good faith, seriously.
We have about six justice bills that are now at various stages, many of them in committee. We just got a new bill today on child pornography, I think a very important bill.
I want to find out from the minister what is the government's intention. This is a dying Parliament. I think we have a couple of weeks left. We are not sitting
next week. We have a week on NAFTA at least. I wonder if it is the government's intention to proceed with these bills or not because we are either going to get no law or we are going to get bad law. I think we should get good law but only with a couple of bills.
I wonder if the government would priorize these bills or indicate its intentions to the opposition in good faith because we will respond in good faith, which bills it really wants to proceed with, which ones it really wants to try to get through the House and how we can help in that way.

Mr. Speaker, before I get into the main body of my remarks, I would like to address the issue that was raised earlier by the New Democratic Party member for Skeena who talked about how the Liberal Party had endorsed the North American free trade agreement. On a point of order, I stood up and challenged him that that was not the case.
Subsequent to his intervention this morning, I want to refer to the specific motion that was put on the floor of the House that day. It was put forward by the hon.
May 13, 1993

member for Kamloops, the NDP government House leader. The motion was:
That this House rejects any North American free trade agreement.
We moved an amendment to that motion. The Liberal amendment was put forward by the member for Etobicoke North, seconded by the member for Ottawa South:
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after
the word "reject" and substituting the following therefor:
- all North American free trade agreements that fail to promote
Canadian workers and jobs, and fail to safeguard the environment.
It was important that I deal with this issue before I get to my remarks because the New Democratic Party member for Skeena when he rose this morning to talk about the motion that was on the floor of the House, talked about people in this House misleading Canadians with their commitments to certain issues.
I believe this is another very specific example where the member for Skeena, by twisting words, tried to cast aspersions on exactly where the Liberal Party of Canada stood when it came to free trade. I believe that Canadians are much more sophisticated than the New Democratic member realizes and I think he will find that out in the next election.
In today's motion we talk about the fact that despite its many grand announcements in international forums and despite the passage of two and a half years since the launch of the green plan, the government has failed to integrate fully environmentally sustainable development as a goal of public policy.
My colleague, the member for Ottawa West, who has put forward this motion is very fair in the sense that she made mention of the many grand announcements of the government. I will give the government credit when it comes to the packaging job it has done on the environment. It has done an outstanding job.
Just about two months ago we all received these green kits "Understanding Our Environment". Of course it has a detailed analysis of what the plan is, what the conceptual design is, in terms of the policy of this government.
Supply
We are not debating the packaging and we are not debating the concept. There is not a government in this world that would not agree with the content of the green plan. What we are talking about is the fact that the government cannot move from the idea stage, from the conceptual stage to the implementation stage. That has been the problem of the government for the last three to four years.
Even in the area of the Small Businesses Loans Act, a good initiative on the part of the government, when it comes to making sure that particular bill, which all of us agreed to in this House, is implemented so that the small business community can get access to it and that the banks will get behind it, it is just not happening.
The thing that concerns me about this lack of action on the environment is that so many young people are missing a tremendous opportunity. I would venture to say that most leaders in industry today who are committed to an environmental ethic have been moved probably more than anything by their children. Children come home from school or college and talk about these issues with their mothers and fathers. We have some of the greatest educational programs in the world right now in our school system in terms of the environment.
In fact I noticed it in this book which is sort of a bible for business. The book is called Green is Gold written by Patrick Carson and Julia Moulden. About a year ago I remember reading in the introduction that one of the inspirations for this particular book came from Richard Currie who was the president of Loblaw Companies Ltd. He mentioned that not only were the environmental issues being reported more frequently in the media, they were popping up in conversations with his children. Of course we all know that the Loblaw companies really led the way in the business community when it came to putting forward their notion of green products and putting a green filter on all the Loblaw companies.
There has been a receptivity to leaders in industry to get involved with the environmental movement out there. I believe that the government has really not used all of its resources to pick up the unemployed youth that are out there.

May 13, 1993
Supply
.(1515)
Let me be very specific and use as an example the Department of Supply and Services, the government purchasing arm in this particular institution. Why would the government purchasing system not set out rules and regulations stating that it will not purchase products or services from Canadian corporations unless they have gone through some kind of an environmental audit to make sure that the company it is dealing with is meeting a certain test in terms of environmental criteria?
Can you imagine the number of jobs that would be taken up overnight, especially by younger people, if it was almost from a moral suasion point of view that young or small companies and businesses became sensitized to the environmental process that is essential if we are going to save this planet? There is a tremendous instrument.
The Department of Supply and Services has offices in every major city and there is absolutely no reason why it could not ask a company to submit its environmental standards, the various environmental activities that it is involved with.
We have about 1.3 billion small businesses in this country. If each and every one of those small businesses treated the environment the same way they treated the books and records of a company, there would not be a small business that would dare try to get through its planning and programming without an accountant. Can you imagine if every small business had an environmental auditor, an environmental consultant, an environmental advisor, somebody in the company that would go through and point out ways in which it could recycle and reuse all the various environmental processes?
This is an area where the government really missed the boat. It could have through a cabinet decision gone to the Department of Supply and Services and said, let us use our leverage to make sure that those who are doing business with us are sensitized to the environmental process to which we are committed.
The other thing I have noticed is there is a lot of young talent out there right now, young entrepreneurs who are putting together environmental resource manuals. I want to refer to one specifically. It is the best one I have seen. It is called The Canadian Environmental Careers Resource Manual. It is a book put together by Noel Desautels in the environmental careers organization.
I want to put on the record that this book is available. It gives advice on career options, career strategies, career counsellors for every sector of the environment, for example science and research, engineering, government service, activism, fine and performing arts, tourism and recreation. It teaches research tips and career planning.
These are the kinds of people that I believe, if we were to engage them in some kind of environmental youth force, a team of environmental rangers, would make sure all the opportunities, all the options related to the environment were put into the marketplace.
Even though we can put these options in opportunities and all of these concepts into the marketplace, ultimately they will only happen if the government uses its influence, its force to sensitize people to the fact that we as a nation are committed to a sustainable environmental program.
When I think back to the very rough period in the country of 1981-82 when we had very high inflation at around 10 per cent and 11 per cent, I remember at that time we were in government and we came out with a program called six and five. The six and five program was a campaign to sensitize people to wage and price restraint.
It was not a regulated program in the business community. However we as a government made sure before we had any kind of relationship with the private sector that it was honouring the basic principles of wage and price restraint, namely the six and five program.
With that program we were able to galvanize the will and the spirit of the nation. In veiy short order we were successful in the collective effort of bringing down inflation and sensitizing people to the fact that we had to constrain our wage demands and make sure that our prices on products and services were back in line.
This is where the government has failed. National standards have really never been part of this government's vision. This government has engaged in a series
May 13, 1993

of dismantling operations that have allowed the provincial governments more and more leverage and power.
All of a sudden we have a situation in which we have 10 different standards and 10 different power brokers all picking away at the national government. It is a very difficult thing to get a national movement going on the environment when the will of the national government has been so fractured.
This is an area of lost opportunity for this government vis-a-vis the environment. When it is all over 17 or 18 weeks from now members of the government will be in their period of reflection as to what things they did wrong. They are going to look back and say: We had a pretty good plan when it came to the green plan. We were on the right track, but what did we do wrong? Why did it fail? Why could we not get people to become a part of that process?
Where this government has failed is in this notion of creating a national movement in which each and every part of the country is part of the whole. Had it used the resources of the national government to say to all its suppliers and all its various relationships that it wants to put a green filter on everyone involved in doing business and interacting with this government then I believe that it probably could have put a million people to work.
This is the one area in our community, in our country or even in the world where we just cannot go wrong. No one is going to turn to a government and condemn it for trying to save the planet, for tiying to reverse the damage that has been going on.
Imagine if this government had 200,000 or 300,000 young people as part of a national environmental youth force. What member of Parliament could stand up and condemn that? Nobody could stand up and condemn that. Just think of the long-term effect that would have had on every part of society. Just think of the impact that would have had in terms of influencing small, mediumsized and large businesses in terms of shifting their habits and attitude.
That is how to create a new paradigm in business, a new type of discipline. We cannot just throw out an idea and wish it to happen. We have to use the resources and the leverage of this government to make sure that our objective is being implemented.
Supply
This government believes that just because it puts a bill through this House of Commons or because it does a press release people are automatically going to follow. There is absolutely no way that happens.
We need accountability. Every 30 or 60 days we have to go out and see how the project is moving along. The bottom line is that this government's conceptual idea in terms of the green plan was a good one. I think it is one of the envies of the world.
The sad story is that it did not move this green plan into the implementation stage.
Who are the losers? Not only is our environment suffering because it is not being attended to, but our economy is suffering and our youth are suffering because they have the talent and the education but they are sitting back and are not a part of the process.
Once again the government has failed to make the connection from a good idea to the implementation stage. Four or five months from now when it is in its period of reflection and meditation as to what went wrong, along with the GST which was a mistake and along with the fact it has not implemented the Small Businesses Loans Act and a lot of other dismantling procedures, it will discover that the area in which it had one of the best ideas but failed to implement it was the green plan.
The biggest disservice the government did was to the youth of Canada because when it comes to the environment our youth in Canada are probably the best qualified in the world. The problem right now is that many of them are sitting at home wondering what to do next and wondering when things are going to start moving again.
All I can say is I hope that within 18 weeks we are going to be able to create that hope once again for the youth of this country. The environmental agenda will be right at the top of our platform.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a brief comment and a question.
In the first part I agree with the hon. member and in the second part I disagree and want to put a question to him. The first part concerns his last couple of sentences in which he said that the young people of Canada are interested in the environment. That is very true.

May 13, 1993
Supply
My riding of Port Moody-Coquitlam, which is about 35 kilometres to the east of Vancouver, nestled up against the coastal mountains, is a very beautiful area. It has been the subject of much development, much housing and new people moving in. It is really the suburbs. It is one of the few areas in Canada that is really growing. In spite of this growth, literally right up the side of mountains houses are going up and forests are being cut, there is an effort in this area by the young people and some other older people who are helping them out to try to preserve some of what used to be there before, specifically the fish.
Coquitlam is an aboriginal word meaning salmon. We have salmon literally going right through some of the new housing developments in the riding. One can actually see salmon spawning in a creek called Noons Creek. Local people have opened up what people thought were closed off sewer outlets and various things and have actually found they can create salmon spawning beds. They can bring back the creeks and they can preserve much of what was a great environment there. It is really quite a noble cause and it is led by the young people.
In the high schools the young people are particularly interested in the environment issue because they recognize that if we do away with all our fish and our animals we will ultimately do away with all the people in the long run. They want to preserve things and at the same time they want to have a liveable community.
I am glad he mentioned that. I think the government could have done more with its green plan. I have tried to go to a number of meetings in my riding with environmental people to encourage them. At the end of this month we are having a conference for people from all over the province dealing with salmon enhancement. It is something very dear to me and a lot of people in British Columbia.
The question I want to put to him is a little nastier. I heard the interchange between him and the member for Skeena. The member for Skeena raised the point that the member for Broadview-Greenwood had voted against the NDP motion, which was against the North American free trade deal, so that the member then had voted in favour of NAFTA.
Perhaps the member could clarify for the House if that was true or not because it is there in the public record. Perhaps he could just briefly tell me if he is for or against NAFTA. Or, is he a traditional Liberal mugwump who wants to be on both sides of the issue at the same time?

Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to deal with the issue of the salmon.
The most polluted river in all of Canada, the Don River, is in my riding. It flows through the centre of the city and into Lake Ontario, which is our drinking water.
We have been working very hard, all levels of government, many people in the private sector, to reclaim the Don River. We hope one day to have salmon in the Don River. We did have the best salmon in Canada not too long ago. Now it is a rare day when people see a salmon and of course they could not eat it.
I hope one day our river can be the same as the rivers that the hon. member talks about in his riding. That is one of the priorities we are focusing on in our community. It is something we are not letting go. We certainly do not consider it a pie in the sky effort.
However I want to deal with NAFTA. I want to tell the hon. member exactly what my position is on NAFTA. It is not a mugwump position or whatever. I do not know what the expression is but the member knows I am a Liberal. I am a party person, but the beautiful thing about the Liberal Party is that it allows for a creative process.
The member for Etobicoke North, our leader on this issue, said that any North American free trade agreement that fails to promote Canadian workers and jobs and fails to safeguard the environment would be a free trade agreement we would not support. It is that simple. We have stated that repeatedly.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Toronto mentioned the Don River. I think everyone would like to see the Don River cleaned up. Maybe he can help me because people have to understand the massive exercise this involves.
While the Don River may empty into lake Ontario at its mouth, studies show that if the government or people were to spend all sorts of money to clean up the industries at the mouth of the Don River it would have a minuscule effect on the pollution in the Don River because the pollution comes from the entire watershed of the Don River.
May 13, 1993

The member mentioned that it involves not just the federal government but the provincial government, and I imagine regional government and municipal townships. I was just wondering, because the member has often provided some intelligence to debates, if he could expand upon that and explain to me the scope of the governments that would have to be involved in the clean-up of just one river in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Cambridge. I consider that a lob ball and I will take it.
The hon. member is absolutely right. It sounds like he knows probably as much or more than I do about the Don River. It is the entire watershed. We are going to need and we are getting co-operation from all levels of government. We have managed in the last five years to have four factories that could not meet the new environmental standards move their buildings away from the Don River.
As a result people, the young and seniors, now walk along the Don River. They are cycling. They are planting trees. More and more people in the community are becoming sensitized to the fact that if we do work together we can reclaim the Don.
The member for Don Valley East has been a tremendous supporter of reclaiming the Don Valley, as have the member for Don Valley West and the member for Rosedale. We have decided we are all working together on this issue.
For me the bottom line is that it is a perfect example of the fact that when we put all of the forces in a common cause together miraculous things can happen.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to point out to the hon. member that I did not want to mislead him or the House. I used the word mugwump. It comes from Mark Twain. It describes someone who has his mug on one side of the fence and his wump on the other. A mugwump is someone who is sitting on the fence. I have tried to answer both sides of the same question.
I applaud what the member said about the Don River. Quiet flows the Don through his riding. I hope they will clean it up.
