You said it used to have the best salmon in Canada. The Fraser River flows by my riding. Could you just say the second best salmon in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I will concede the second best as long as he will concede that he understands exactly where I stand on NAFTA. If we do not get the environmental amendments, labour standards and all the things we have mentioned in this House, then he knows exactly where I stand on the issue.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon to speak to this opposition motion. I must say I am somewhat surprised at the wording of the motion because I expected the opposition to condemn the government outright for its policy on sustainable development and the environment. However there is some indication at least in the wording that it only regrets. To quote the motion, despite many grand announcements, the government has taken some action. The government has failed to integrate fully environmentally sustainable development, all of which gives the impression that the opposition has raised an interesting point for discussion this afternoon but seems to admit, by its wording of the motion that, all things considered, the present government has not failed to meet its commitments.
Speaking as an average citizen who also happens to be the member for Richmond-Wolfe and vice-chairman of the Standing Committee on Environment, I would like to start by quoting from an article in the Calgary Herald, which I would like to read to you:

"The other political parties regularly enjoy dumping on the green plan but the policy in reality is that since its unveiling in December, 1990 it has become the centrepiece of the national environmental debate and the yardstick against which private activists and political critics must be measured".

That being said, I would like to say first of all that Canada's green plan, announced by the federal government on December 11, 1990, constitutes the government's strategy and national action plan on sustainable development. It was prepared after massive consulta-

May 13, 1993
Supply
tions with Canadians from all walks of life: governments, business, special interest groups and the general public.
The purpose of the green plan was to secure for current and future generations a safe and healthy environment and a sound and prosperous economy. This perspective implies a fundamental change in the way the government looks at economic development and the environment. Both are inextricably linked and are essential to the health and well-being of all Canadians.
While providing a framework for action on a series of specific problems, from ozone depletion to protecting our national heritage, the green plan deals with the very basis for sustainable development: the need to make this a principal part of decision making at all levels of society.
The green plan also provides the basis for new, stronger partnerships for sustainable development. We all have a role to play in meeting environmental challenges. We must all work together if we want sustainable development to become a reality.
Canada's green plan represents the federal government's response to this challenge. It is based on the following elements: first, the concept of sustainable development which implies reconciling our economic needs with the ability of the environment to support present and future generations.
Second, it is an exhaustive plan, a consistent set of measures covering a broad range of environmental issues from global warming to wildlife and parks.
Third, it is a plan that commits all government departments. It acknowledges that environmental issues are not bound by the traditional barriers between departments and that a concerted effort by all departments is essential if we are to respond effectively to environmental challenges.
The green plan assumes that substantial new resources will be earmarked for the environment. At a time when spending on most other programs will diminish or be capped at current levels, funding for the green plan will continue to grow substantially from year to year. That is very important.
In the green plan's first year, for instance, we spent $210 million at the federal level. We spent $286 million the next year and $351 million has been budgeted for the year after. The trend is clear.
Because of the extent and urgency of the challenges involved, the green plan is one of the sectors where spending is accelerating. The plan contains a broad range of specific objectives and time frames setting out the government's accountability, and I will name a few.
First is a reduction of smog concentrations across Canada to bring them below levels at which they are harmful to the most vulnerable groups in our population. Second is a 50 per cent reduction by the year 2000 in the quantity of waste we produce. Third is forest management not only in terms of economic yield but in terms of sustainable development. Fourth, the plan aims at setting aside 12 per cent of our territory for nature reserves. Fifth, it aims at completing our network of national parks by the year 2000. Sixth, it provides for stabilizing greenhouse gases at their 1990 levels by the year 2000. And finally, its objective is the gradual elimination of CFCs or chlorofluorocarbons, and other substances that deplete the ozone layer.
All these objectives and time frames are extremely important for the implementation of the green plan. I think this reflects the government's determination to announce its objectives and to explain how it intends to meet those objectives.
Because of its perspective on sustainable development, Canada has been praised throughout the world for its green plan. It is also why the then director general of the United Nations Environment Program described the green plan as a model for the rest of the world.
As indicated in the report on the plan's second year published last March, real progress has been achieved despite the usual constraints, including financial jurisdiction and other problems.
Today Canada's green plan is entering its third year. Since it came into force, we have been improving the decision-making process which lies at the heart of sustainable development. For instance, the Environmental Assessment Act received royal assent last June. This is a key factor in the federal government's general strategy for putting its house in order. It isn't easy, when
May 13, 1993

we consider the many federal and provincial jurisdictions.
After committing itself to the process, the government produced an environmental assessment of the North American free trade agreement. This is the first time environmental considerations have been part of trade negotiations. I may add that in the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement there was less emphasis on such measures. However in NAFTA the process is well under way. This is another example of our efforts, the increasing awareness of our trading partners and of course Canada's leadership in this respect. Furthermore, certain regulations applying to pulp and paper mills are now in effect. I know what I am talking about because I come from a riding where we have Kruger in Bromptonville and Domtar in Windsor which both have major pulp and paper plants. It took a number of years to develop and negotiate these regulations, which are based on sound scientific data.
A working paper on economic instruments was also produced. We are talking about a first step towards using market forces to guarantee environmental protection.
Finally, a second report on the state of the environment was published last year with accurate, useful and accessible information to help Canadians make enlightened decisions. I could also mention the code of environmental stewardship for federal government activities which was adopted recently.
Clearly the green plan has done a lot to clean up the environment and make sustainable development a guiding principle that reconciles economic development with environmental protection, both here and abroad.
From the Atlantic coast to the Fraser Valley and the Arctic shores, Canadians are working together to meet the objectives set by the green plan for a cleaner, safer and healthier environment. For instance, in the Atlantic provinces 13 communities are developing plans for management of their inshore resources. Each project is organized and directed at the local level, which is very important. We are getting down to the nitty-gritty.
Supply
In Quebec, the Centre interuniversitaire de recherche et toxicologie, run by the University of Montreal and the University of Quebec in Montreal, is affiliated with a national network that examines the effects of toxic chemical substances on living organisms. Are those half-measures? Is this an example of the government's failure to act on the environment? I think we agree these examples are proof of the opposite, but there is more.
In Ontario, the automobile industry has set up a complete pollution prevention program aimed at voluntary Canada-wide reduction of use, production and disposal of toxic substances.
In the Prairies, each province is creating living models of sustainable forest management, thanks to partnerships involving government, industry, aboriginal groups, universities and other parties. Each model forest is part of a national network that will establish a new relationship between forest management and the environment. Do you want more examples, Mr. Speaker?
In British Columbia a large number of partners are working together on a sustainable development plan for the Fraser River, in order to clean up contaminated sites, stop pollution, restore wildlife habitat and salmon populations, and improve water quality. This plan served as the starting point for the federal-provincial-municipal agreement signed in May 1992.
In the north, with its fragile ecosystem, a team of students has removed dangerous and unsightly waste accumulated during the past 50 years or more on the shores and islands of Great Slave Lake as part of a project set up by the Metis nation in the Northwest Territories.
As Canadians we should be proud of our efforts and applaud these achievements. These are some concrete examples of the slogan: think globally, act locally.
The earth summit was a major event for the cause of sustainable development in 1992. We did more than act locally. There was a meeting in Rio, with consultations and dialogue. In fact, thanks to its green plan, Canada came to the summit well prepared to contribute to global change. I would like to mention the magnificent performance by our Minister of the Environment who led the Canadian delegation and was also foremost among

May 13, 1993
Supply
the committed participants at this summit. Canada went to Rio eager to learn more, as did other countries.
The past two years have shown that the basic principles of the green plan are as valid today as they were in 1990. However, the plan was meant to evolve with the times because nothing is ever perfect.
We must therefore ensure that it will continue to meet the new needs which will arise and that it will enable us to benefit from the experience gained. Our greatest priority must be to make better use of the whole range of available means of environmental protection. First and foremost there is the promotion of voluntary measures. There is also the use of market forces to influence millions of collective and individual decisions. Finally there is rationalizing the activities of the different levels of government in Canada.
Our second priority concerns the economic dimension of sustainable development. The business community is a key partner in making new connections between the environment and the economy in Canada. We see that it is not easy to connect or join all these partners or participants in different communities and different activities. The green plan is meant to promote the emergence of an environmentally competitive private sector.
Our third priority is to broaden the scope of the green plan so we can handle the comprehensive aspects of sustainable development, for example by integrating environmental issues in multilateral trade negotiations and by helping developing countries make the transition to sustainable development. We have a responsibility in this regard. Things are going on not only in our country but abroad as well. We must share this expertise or even the environmental problems we had by passing on reports and findings and of course encouraging our partners in developing countries to join us. In this way the whole planet will be made aware and can find common solutions and be healthier for it.
If you allow me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about another initiative in Quebec which is considered an example in many fields and in which, as member for a riding in that province, I have a special interest like many other citizens. It concerns the St. Lawrence River, a major route in eastern Canada.
The federal government has undertaken to protect the river so that, like us and our grandparents, future generations can enjoy this major waterway. Five years ago in June 1988 the Prime Minister of Canada announced a $110 million investment to clean up the St. Lawrence River.
That was the beginning of the St. Lawrence Action Plan. At the time this plan was considered ambitious, even daring by some on account of its objectives, because it was claimed that the federal government had decided with the Government of Quebec to tackle the pollution caused by 50 businesses considered priorities. This plan was thought to be audacious. Today some say that it is not daring enough. We must be logical.
On April 2 the Minister of the Environment announced in Quebec City that the Government of Canada had decided to invest $100 million over the next five years in implementing phase II of the St. Lawrence plan. These funds will make it possible to continue the achievements of the first phase of the plan.
Let me remind the House of the objectives which have been realized under this St. Lawrence plan between 1988 and 1993. The conservation of 5,000 hectares of wildlife habitat along the river is now assured. The Saguenay Marine Park was created. Survival plans for six endangered species including beluga whales were implemented. The restoration of some federal properties along the St. Lawrence, in particular the Lachine Canal and the national ports, was begun. Are these not important activities, decisions and actions all along the St. Lawrence? I think that mentioning them shows the awareness and responsibility and that these action plans in the green plan will soon succeed.
Thanks to this St. Lawrence plan, new environmental technologies have been developed. Phase I of the action plan helped develop a leading edge industry in Quebec and Canada. According to a study by Cogesult, phase I helped create or maintain some 2,200 jobs a year between 1988 and 1993 and generated $1.4 billion in economic benefits. This is an outstanding performance and an outstanding result. By March 1993 liquid toxic waste dumped in the river by the 50 businesses considered priorities had been reduced 74 per cent. These results have had a significant environmental impact. The goal of 90 per cent will be reached in 1995.
May 13, 1993

Mr. Speaker, you see that this illustrates what this government did to implement a plan that was considered daring and helped achieve the results which I described earlier.

Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to congratulate the member for Richmond-Wolfe on this fine attempt to defend the policies advocated by his government in the past two or three years, especially those arising from the green plan.
Of course some good things have been done. Ecologists for example argue that there is no such thing as surplus water, that all the water in an ecosystem plays a vital role and its removal can and will cause irreversible damage.
There have been discussions for example as to whether small scale water diversions or collecting water as it spills out into coastal estuaries will affect the environment. A good example is the removal of fresh water inflows from coastal estuaries, as I mentioned just a moment ago. Another good example is the tanker exports from Toba Inlet off the west coast of British Columbia. Those kinds of exports can have a dramatic impact on the marine populations for literally hundreds of kilometres seaward. We really do not have any knowledge of the kind of environmental impact that is invoked when we start removing water from an ecosystem. Alterations of fresh water flows from Hudson Bay, for example, a result of the James Bay project, have been shown to affect salinity and marine productivity as far away from James Bay as the Grand Banks off Newfoundland. The fact is that Agriculture Canada was involved in sustainable development long before it became fashionable. For example, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration, better known as PFRA, which was established in 1935 is all about soil and water conservation.
It was established to deal with the effects of the droughts of the 1930s but it has adapted with the times and now includes large water resource development projects, irrigation demonstrations and shelter belts. Through the years the PFRA has given away nearly 550 million seedlings for shelter belts.
PFRA promoted farm management strategies developed by the forerunner to Agriculture Canada's research branch. Some of the branch's more recent successes include a sterile insect release program in British Columbia that eliminates costly spraying, and experiments in Alberta that are proving the benefits of reduced tillage especially in dry years when yields are increased as much as 30 per cent.
Environmental sustainability was one of the four pillars of the Agricultural Food Policy Review launched in 1989 by the then Minister of Agriculture. This led to the creation of a federal-provincial industry task force that produced recommendations to take our agri-food sector to the year 2000.
I would be remiss if I did not mention that this report was hailed by environmental groups and farm groups alike. Ducks Unlimited said it was the finest environmental action plan ever produced by government.
Over the years Agriculture Canada has responded to the need to protect our environment and promote sustainable development with a number of programs.
The National Soil Conservation Program that just ended in March was a 50:50 cost-shared federal-provincial program. The federal government contributed more than $75 million through this program to promote the best use of soil resources to sustain productivity.
The Land Management Assistance Program provided over $22 million of federal funds from 1991-92 to 1993-94 to the seven non-prairie provinces to facilitate
the adoption of effective lands resource management and environmentally sustainable farming practices.
The Permanent Cover Program provided over $70 million in direct cash payments to producers since 1988 to take marginal lands out of production. The conversion of these lands to permanent cover will result in soil conservation and wildlife habitat benefits to producers. It will also give producers an alternate source of income.
More than $12 million of federal spending went into the Soil and Water Environmental Enhancement Program in Ontario. This six-year program which has just ended was aimed at reducing phosphorus loading into the Lake Erie basin. An evaluation will be available later this summer.
That long list of projects forms a prelude to the green plan. The green plan is the flagship environmental program for the department. It carries the momentum of these projects forward to 1996-97. Through the green plan we are working with the provinces and industry to protect the natural resources that agriculture needs to remain viable.
One hundred and fifty-five million dollars will be spent on green plan activities aimed at soil conservation, water quality, managing farm waste and pollution, pesticides, integrating agriculture and wildlife, biodiversity and climate change.
The federal government has so far signed green plan agreements with six of the provinces and territories, or maybe that should be seven now. A signing was scheduled to take place in British Columbia at one p.m. our time and there will be another signing tomorrow in New Brunswick.
This is what Noel Brown, North American director for the United Nations Environment Program, had to say about the green plan. He said: "What impresses the world is that one country can formulate for itself a coherent vision of a sustainable future". He called Canada's green plan a model for other nations.
A few years ago the Prime Minister made a commitment that the federal government would conduct environmental assessments not only on all the projects but also of all policies and programs.
When the House passed the Farm Income Protection Act in 1991, the legislation that enabled us to create our farm safety nets GRIP and NISA, it included built-in provisions for ongoing environmental assessment. This
May 13, 1993

was a first for federal legislation. In addition to GRIP and NISA, an environmental assessment of the Western Grain Transportation Act has been completed.
I have spoken about the past and the present so I would like to conclude with a few words about the future.
It is common practice to conduct economic assessments of proposed government policies, but we have little experience in doing environmental assessments because we have lacked the tools. This is changing. Agriculture Canada is actively involved in developing environmental indicators that will help us to gauge progress in moving toward environmental sustainability in the sector.
The department is also preparing to meet the new legislative requirements of Bill C-13, the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act.
Finally, Speaker, Agriculture Canada is continuing its role in further developing its capacity to conduct environmental reviews of its policies.

The member for Delta says everything is hunky-doiy, those big bad people in the opposition over there are just getting all worked up again and spreading lies about us good people because we did not do things.
May 13, 1993

I would like to have his comments on what the Minister of the Environment has had to say about the issue. Let me read what he said in a letter dated February 17, 1993, after seven paragraphs of trying to explain to his colleague what the government is up to. He then gets around to saying in paragraph eight: By the way, I, the Minister of the Environment, would appreciate if you, the minister of fisheries, having been ordered to do so by cabinet in July 1987, and having been re-ordered to do it in December 1990-he says this on February 17, 1993. Now I am going to quote him directly because what I just said was a bit of a rough paraphrase, as I am known to do from time to time.
Here are the actual words from the pen of the Minister of the Environment: "I would appreciate learning of your intentions regarding the release of a public discussion paper on this important legislative initiative". He is saying: Tell us what you are going to do. What about your discussion paper? Ah, I forgot. What discussion paper?
I failed to mention that part of the cabinet order was that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans have the discussion paper ready by the end of 1991. Fourteen months later, or six years after all those great intentions were expressed, one minister is writing to another fellow who sits all of 30 feet from him. He takes two pages to explain to him what it is all about. He says: In case you didn't know it, minister of fisheries, we have a green plan; in case you didn't know it, we would like to have an oceans act; in case you didn't know it, we made those decisions six years ago; in case you didn't know it, we made them all over again two and a half years ago; in case you didn't know it, we have been waiting for 14 months for your paper, in case you didn't know it, minister of fisheries.
Is it any wonder that my friend from Ottawa West put in her motion:
That this House regrets that, despite many grand announcements in international forums and despite the passage of two and a half years since the launch of the green plan, the government has failed -
I guess it has. The Minister of the Environment says it has. There is his letter. He cannot even get one of his own colleagues to tell him what he plans to do as a result of a government decision that was taken six years ago in another month or so, in July.
Supply
The road to hell is paved with good intentions. With the track record of this crowd the Conservatives will probably get the paving contract. They have to be the absolute experts at road paving when it comes to intentions. This is a matter that deserves a much better response from government than that.
What has been the real response of government? Six days ago, last Thursday, I was in the House of Commons committee on fisheries with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. We had our usual little friendly chat, as we are known to do. He is a very personable fellow. I asked him during the committee proceedings about this letter. I asked him why his colleague, the Minister of the Environment, was ganging up on him. I asked him why after so many months, 14 of them had passed since the deadline for doing this discussion paper, he had not got around to doing it.
I just happen to have with me the transcript of what the minister and I had to say to each other that particular day. He said: "It is not a matter that I have been able to give a lot of attention to".
With regard to oceans dumping, the Oceans Act, the discussion paper, the letters I am getting from the Minister of the Environment on the issue about sound environmental policy, he said: "That is not a matter I have been able to give much attention to. I have not had time for it. I have more important things on my plate". I guess he has.
We have something called foreign overfishing. I suppose that is still on his plate unless it slipped onto the table and then onto the floor. I have not heard much from him about it lately. Maybe he has a big plate and cannot see it and cannot find it.
There are no shortage of grand announcements about that either but as I stand here and as you, Mr. Speaker, sit here the fact is that today at this point in time there are 99 by actual count foreign boats 200 miles east of St. John's on those two little projections of the continental shelf. Those two projections extend just beyond the 200-mile limit.
One is called the nose of the Grand Banks because it looks like a nose. I have not been there but they tell me it looks like a nose. I take their word for it. The other projection a little farther to the south is called the tail because I am told it resembles a tail of a fish. The nose and tail of the Grand Banks are two projections of the

May 13, 1993
Supply
continental shelf just beyond the 200-mile limit east of St. John's, Newfoundland.
Today at this hour in the evening 99 boats-on any day there are around 100 boats-from other countries are out there fishing. What are they fishing? Some of them are fishing the very species that our fishermen are not allowed to fish. Right now Canadian taxpayers are spending quite a large sum of money to compensate fishermen and plant workers on the northeast coast of Newfoundland because of a northern cod moratorium.
Let us understand what we are talking about. The fish they are getting paid not to catch are the same fish that those boats are out there catching. It is the same fish. What kind of a cock-eyed policy is that?
These people ought to be compensated if the government has stepped in and prevented them from going to work. Nobody has an argument with that practice. That is not the issue. Those plant workers and fishermen are prevented from going to work through no fault of their own but because of a government fiat, a government decision which said in effect tomorrow morning you cannot work for two years.
Once the government takes that kind of a decision on behalf of all the people of Canada then it has an obligation. It is fulfilling that obligation to compensate those people. That is not the issue. The issue is why in the name of everything that is sane, that is environmentally sound, this government is sitting idly by and allowing boats, some of them without even a quota to be out there today, to further pillage stock that is already under such serious threat that we in this country have had to declare a moratorium for two years. As the minister said the other day, two years is not going to be enough. If the boats continue out there no time will be enough.
If this government wants to beat its breast about its environmental policy and all the good things it has done in this particular area it ought first for the sake of people all over this world, eveiy maritime nation on earth, put its money where its mouth is when it comes to the pillaging of that great resource off Newfoundland.
If there was ever a clear case, if there was ever international unanimity on an issue, it is the issue that
we ought not to pillage our marine resources because they belong to all generations. This generation has an obligation to ensure that they are there for the next generation.
What better, more graphic, more immediate example of sustainable development would you want than one that in its practice can nurture the jobs of thousands and in its abuse can spell the end to a very precious marine resource and with it the end to a rural way of life which has sustained people in my province and in Atlantic Canada for 500 years?
I see by your signal that my time is up. I thank you for your patience.

Mr. Speaker, I want to acknowledge the remarks of my colleague for Burin-St. George's. I also want to say that our colleague for Ottawa West organized a constructive debate today. It was not all critical. We naturally have a responsibility as Her Majesty's loyal opposition to point out some of the flaws in the system. The government cannot think that everything that it is doing is on the right track.
One of the really sad things that is happening in our country today is that the good ideas do not seem to have access to the process. Right now, this day, this minute as we speak, on the front lawn of Parliament Hill the Canadian Auto Workers have a display. It is a graveyard of the 300 to 400 companies that have been affected adversely by the free trade agreement.
I was talking to Ed Gould who works at one of the plants in St. Catharines about the environment. He told me that if in the plant where he works in St. Catharines there had just been a little more creativity put to use that plant could have been an environmental recycling plant. Instead of having the loss of all those jobs and people going on UI and on welfare, they could have brought in some recycling technology.
These craftspeople from this particular General Motors plant are familiar with the whole aspect of putting a car together and taking it apart. This could have been a tremendous world-class recycling plant to which old cars from all over North America could have been brought. That would have kept workers in that community, that plant, that labour force viable as taxpayers rather than being on unemployment insurance and welfare.
May 13, 1993

We kept hearing one common theme as we went through this debate, that there are a lot of good ideas and a lot of innovations which exist. Somehow our process of listening to or putting these ideas into the implementation phase is very weak.
I see the minister responsible for one of the most efficient departments of government, the Department of Supply and Services, in the House. It has always been a good, efficient department. In the few weeks left it might be interesting to review that department's capability. They tend to have a business flare in that department. Maybe that department could be the department for accessing innovation on new ideas which are linked to the environment.
I have the highest respect-

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
subsubtopic: PROCLAMATION OF PARTS II AND III
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should immediately proclaim parts II and III of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act, which was passed by the House of Commons on June 25, 1986.
He said: I hope that during the course of the consideration of this motion there will be more attention paid by members of the government than appears to be visible at this juncture.
It would appear to me that this is the degree of attention the cabinet has given to proclamation for the past seven years, ever since this House of Commons
Private Members' Business
passed the Parliamentary Employees and Staff Relations Act in June 1986, just one month short of seven years ago.
Many times I have asked the government why it has taken seven years to proclaim a law it introduced to this House of Commons which was passed by all parties. The most controversial section of it, namely part I, was proclaimed almost seven years ago. Why has it not proceeded to proclaim the other operative sections, parts II and III? They simply would provide to the some 3,000 or 3,500 employees of the House of Commons, no matter what kind of work they do, the same very basic labour standards legislation and occupational health and safety legislation which all other employees in Canada under federal jurisdiction enjoy.
I would just like to pontificate for a moment on a couple of possible reasons. There may be some misunderstanding about what the bill does. Some members may think that parts II and III have something to do with the unionisation of the parliamentary staff in their own offices. That is not the case.
Part I, which was already proclaimed, dealt with union recognition and certification of unions on Parliament Hill but it specifically excluded those employees who worked directly under the supervision of senators and members of Parliament. Therefore that is not an issue.
Maybe some members are concerned that their own office staff who, some might argue, are akin to executive assistants of cabinet ministers and political appointees should not be covered by union recognition or certification. There may be that argument and it has some legitimacy.
Maybe they think the inclusion of their employees under parts II and III is somehow going to restrict their ability to run an efficient operation. These employees would not be excluded by parts II and III which cover basic labour standards and occupational health and safety.
If we allowed any other employer in the country to say that the most basic laws governing hours of work and payment of wages are going to create problems then we would have no labour standards and no health and safety legislation across this country at all.
I would suggest that it is absolutely ridiculous for anybody to argue, and I have not heard anybody here argue it, that those basic labour standards and basic

May 13, 1993
Private Members' Business
occupational health and safety protective measures should not be accorded to all Canadians.
Then perhaps tongue in cheek the answer is to be found in those long-time definitions of the terms progressive and conservative. Progressives have been defined in the past with some degree of legitimacy as people who believe that things ought to be done for the first time. Conservatives are those who believe that maybe they should be but not now. Perhaps that explains the seven-year gestation period when we have been waiting to see the birth of this legislation which the government introduced and we all passed.
There have been repeated questions, statements, petitions, letters and phone calls to all members of the House of Commons of all parties from people right across the country for the last seven years and still no movement.
In answer to repeated questions, both by mail and verbally in this House and in personal conversations we have yet to hear the government give one single substantive reason why it has not proceeded. The government House leader did answer a question of mine on March 23, which I regard as almost a mischievous answer. He said: "Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the government we say that it is not really the government that is holding up this issue. This issue deals exclusively with the House of Commons, with employees of the House of Commons and with employees of individual members. There are certain aspects of the law which would impose on individual members some requirements that there has been some reluctance to take on. The proper forum to discuss this is the Board of Internal Economy. I will certainly relay the hon. member's concerns to the board".
He went on to answer in a supplementary by saying: "This is not a government question. It is a House of Commons question. There is a distinction. The Board of Internal Economy has the responsibility for this and the hon. member's party has a representative on the Board of Internal Economy. If there was such indignation in the NDP caucus all these years, why was it never raised by the hon. member's representative?"
The answer to that is that it was raised many times over the past several years by the member for Kamloops,
the House leader of the NDP. The answer has always been the same: "It is not our business. We do not proclaim legislation. The government has never asked us to study the matter", and so they say it is not their responsibility. It is not their concern. It has not been referred to them except by the NDP House leader, contrary to the assertions of the government House leader.
Just last night, to be sure once again, it was placed on the agenda of the Board of Internal Economy. It did not have time to deal with it last night. It did not seem to think it was urgent enough and other items took precedence. That is fine and maybe properly so, but after seven years surely somebody has to give some consideration to it.
I have written to the Speaker, I have written to the Prime Minister and I have written to the president of the Privy Council. I have asked questions of the government House leader. We have raised it on the Board of Internal Economy and we have yet to get one substantive reason why, after almost seven full years-just one month short-the government simply refuses to take any action which would lead to the proclamation of this basic health and safety legislation and basic labour standards legislation for those who work for us in this House of Commons.
We know them personally. Surely we all agree they are Canadians who are deserving of the same basic protection as other Canadians. Contrary to some public opinion, many of those employees engage in occupations which constitute some hazards to themselves, their fellow workers and the rest of us who work in and around this place.
Surely for our protection as well as their protection and the public's protection who visit us here, either on vacation or on business, they should have the same right to participate, for instance, in joint management, employee-employer health and safety committees as happens in every other operation across Canada under federal jurisdiction and in most provincial jurisdictions. Whether those operations are organized and unionized or whether they are non-unionized, all employees under the Canada Labour Code within federal jurisdiction have the right to participate in discussing matters relating to their own health and safety.
May 13, 1993

Whoever is answering for the government in this discussion I hope finally will give one substantive reason why after almost seven years this legislation, parts II and III of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act, has not been proclaimed.
In the last few weeks there have been innumerable letters to members of Parliament of all parties, phone calls, petitions presented in the House of Commons. Just last night I addressed a membership meeting of the Public Service Alliance of Canada employees on the Hill and I was assured by them that they have been in touch with many members of Parliament of all parties. They get a lot of sympathy and understanding but no one from any party, including the government party, can give them a reason why we have not proceeded. It boggles the mind and one wonders just where we can go from here.
The present Governor General of Canada was government House leader when this question came before a parliamentary committee back in 1986.1 want to read the remarks of His Excellency, then the government House leader, to that committee.
Mr. Chairman and members, in order to put the provisions of Bill C-45 -
That was the number of the bill at that time.
- in their appropriate context I would like to briefly review for the committee the events leading up to the tabling of this important legislation.
Collective bargaining for parliamentary employees has been the topic of discussion for many years. In 1967, a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons recommended that the employees of Parliament be given bargaining rights similar to those being accorded to public servants under Bill C-170.
In 1982 the Privy Council Office commissioned a study of the matter by Mr. Robert Weir. His report was tabled in February 1983 and outlined a number of options.
With the assistance of the Privy Council Office the Management and Members Services Committee of the House of Commons prepared a draft act which was accepted unanimously by representatives of all three political parties.
In March 1984 the chairman of the Management and Members Services Committee of the House of Commons requested that the government of the day prepare legislation based on the draft act which envisioned limited collective bargaining rights for employees of the Senate, the House of Commons, and Library of Parliament. It was modelled on the Public Service Staff Relations Act but with no right to strike included in the legislation.
Private Members' Business
The former government did not introduce legislation as requested by the committee prior to the general election of 1984. However, in August 1984 my predecessor as President of the Privy Council, the Hon. Andre Ouellet, publicly announced his intention if the previous government had been re-elected to bring forward the bill which had received all-party support in March 1984.
Immediately upon my appointment as government House leader I turned my attention to this important issue. The tabling of Bill C-45 on April 30, 1985 represented the first positive action by any government to accord collective bargaining rights to employees of Parliament.
As hon. members of this committee are aware, the bill which I have sponsored goes beyond the model originally proposed by the Management and Members Services Committee in that it also incorporates, and this is in addition to the draft bill which has been the subject of all-party agreement, the protections of Parts III and IV of the Canada Labour Code dealing with labour standards and occupational safety and health respectively.
In addition political staffs of members of Parliament and senators as well as all employees on the Hill regardless of employment or whether or not they are in a union, all members will be entitled to the protection of Parts III and IV of the code.
This initiative to provide parliamentary employees with labour legislation tailored to the special circumstances of their employment has unfortunately been delayed by events which take place in another forum.
In late 1983 the unions which had been endeavouring to represent the employees of Parliament approached the Canada Labour Relations Board seeking certification. In April 1984 the board determined that it had jurisdiction. Hearings were held, appropriate bargaining units determined and a number of certification orders were issued.
What all that shows is there was all the consultation in the world. The now Governor General, the then government House leader, said very clearly that this matter had been discussed with all members, with the management service and with the members services committee for years. He went so far as to say then that it was a shame it had taken so long to get to that point.
Almost seven years later we are still waiting. Those two most basic provisions, those that should be the least controversial, those which simply accord basic health and safety rights and basic labour standard rights such as hours of work, payment of wages, et cetera, still have not been proclaimed.
The last correspondence I received was in answer to a question which the current President of the Privy Council took as notice when I asked him in this House about the matter on April 30. It is a very short response and most of it is simply a re-cataloguing of what the question

May 13, 1993
Private Members' Business
is. The President of the Privy Council states in his letter of May 12:
The question concerns the working conditions of employees of Members of Parliament as well as other employees of the House, the Senate and the Library of Parliament. Part II of the PESRA provides for such matters as maximum hours of work, minimum wages, holidays and leave entitlements under the Canada Labour Code. Part III provides that the Canada Labour Code provisions on health and safety standards apply to all Parliament Hill employees. These issues and their implications for all MPs are of direct concern to the Board of Internal Economy as the Government House Leader pointed out in his response to you during Question Period on March 23, 1993.
The Board of Internal Economy is an all-party forum for discussion and resolution of administration matters related to the House of Commons. The Government would want to consider the views of the Board before proceeding to implement the PESRA changes.
Yours sincerely,
It was signed by the President of the Privy Council.
If the government for the last seven years wanted to consider the views of the board before proceeding to proclaim these two vety simple parts that are common to employees across the country, why has it not asked? Why has it not at any point referred it to the Board of Internal Economy? Why have the only people who have raised it with the board, been told by the board that it is not their business, been representatives of the NDP and the NDP House leader?
Either the government did not know what it was doing seven years ago in 1986, after all of that discussion and all of that consideration, or it simply does not know what the heck it is doing now. People are frustrated. The people who work for us and all Canadians in this place are frustrated. We have had suicides recently, partly due we are told to stress on the job and other kinds of problems. We have had major problems over the last several years with asbestos in the House. The absence of any structured employee-employer health and safety committees to discuss that has led to all kinds of rumours, all kinds of problems that we maybe do not even have because we do not have a structured way of dealing with these problems.
My question to the government simply is: if it will not give consent to let this come to a vote now and vote again
on what we voted in favour of seven years ago, will it at least give a clear substantive answer to what is the problem? Why will it not proclaim parts II and III? If it wants to hear from the Board of Internal Economy, why has it not asked it what the problems are?
We really do not know where to go from here. I ask for unanimous consent to have this motion deemed as votable. If that is denied I hope that the least that we can afford for those who work for us and all Canadians in this House of Commons is to give a clear answer why, after seven years, the government has done nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
subsubtopic: PROCLAMATION OF PARTS II AND III
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this debate on motion No. M-743 moved by my hon. colleague from Kootenay West-Revelstoke.
The hon. member would have the government proclaim immediately parts II and III of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act. This act, commonly called Bill C-45, was tabled in this House on April 30, 1985. It was read the third time and passed on June 25, 1986 and part I was proclaimed on December 24, 1986.
This act deals with employment in the Senate, the House of Commons and the parliamentary library. It has three parts, the first of which has been in force for several years and sets the negotiating rights of employees of the House, the Senate and the Library with the exception of the immediate staff of members and senators. Part II deals with standard hours, minimum wages, leave and statutory holidays and covers all parliamentary employees. It does this through the Canada Labour Code provisions. Part III states that all parliamentary employees are covered by the Canada Labour Code provisions on occupational safety and health.

May 13, 1993

First, I would like to point out that many parliamentary employees presently enjoy working conditions that are identical to those prescribed in the Labour Code and even better in some cases. I am talking here about employees covered by collective agreements as well as employees that are non-unionized but whose working conditions are defined. In fact, those employees are already covered by part II of the Staff Relations Act.
For a specific group of parliamentary employees, that is those who work for MPs and senators, the motion brought forward today is very significant. It deals with some essential elements of the unique working relationship that exists between MPs and senators and their staff. As soon as parts II and III of the act are proclaimed, the provisions of the legislation concerning hours of work, annual leave, statutory holidays, sick leave, bereavement leave, maternity leave, child care leave, sexual harassment, health and safety and grievances procedure could be applied to MPs staff.
That does not mean that on Parliament Hill those matters are not already dealt with by other legal provisions. The question is whether or not the provisions of the Canada Labour Code are appropriate in all circumstances considering the unique workplace that Parliament Hill is.
I am not convinced that the impacts or the proclamation of parts II and III of the act were reviewed seriously enough. My suggestion is to take a few minutes to discuss certain changes that should be made to the rules governing members' employees if the last two parts of this bill are proclaimed.
To begin with, there is the issue of working hours and overtime. Presently there is no restriction on the number of hours of work in a week for members' employees. Part II of the act repeats the wording found in part III of the Canada Labour Code, which states that no employee can work more than 48 hours a week without the formal approvals of Labour Canada. Let's face it. When Parliament sits it is not necessarily from 9 to 5, far from it. When the House sits, members need support services that are provided by their employees.
Another example has to do with overtime. Presently, although members's employees do not get any overtime pay, members may grant compensatory leave either on a straight time or a time and a half basis for each hour
Private Members' Business
worked overtime at their discretion. The Canada Labour Code also governs overtime and requires compensation at least on a time and a half basis for each hour of work over eight hours a day or forty hours a week.
After a closer look, we find that these amendments could be impossible to implement and that some rules could not be applicable to members' staff. We would all agree, I think, that our workload is extremely variable, heavy when the House is sitting, lighter when it is not. Therefore the Labour Code uniform regulations might be impracticable.
I think other aspects have to be considered too. We need to ask where the funds to pay this overtime will come from. How will we cover these expenses that could surely be very heavy? Do hon. members have the necessary budgets? If not, how will we finance these additional expenses? I think it is fair to say that is very disturbing. Our parliamentary responsibilities are so fundamental that nothing should come in their way.
We must ask if the proclamation of parts II and III of the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act will not result in a lesser flexibility. I think we must remember that Parliament is not an ordinary employer. We may have to maintain part of the flexibility we now have. I think all members realize that there are times when every hour counts and, once the work is finished, the employee can be granted leave as compensation. Is this not a better and more flexible approach considering the nature of our work?
Let us look at what is implied in terms of annual leave in the new legislation. Again, it is an area where we enjoy some flexibility at the moment. Employees who work for MPs receive, in lieu of leave, a lump sum equivalent to 4 per cent of the previous year's pay for those who have less than six years of continuous employment, and to 6 per cent of the previous year's pay for those who have more than six years of continuous employment. Moreover, MPs may grant other paid leave at their discretion, which they do. In many cases, an employee gets three or four weeks of leave plus a lump sum.
Part II of the legislation would grant all employees working for MPs two weeks of annual leave, during which they will receive a salary equivalent to 4 per cent of that year's gross earnings, including overtime. After six years of employment, the rate would increase to 6 per cent.

Private Members' Business
As I said earlier, several employees already get the annual leave and the lump sum. What good would changing the leave plan do? Do the new clauses put these employees at a disadvantage? Should we limit the discretion allowed members of Parliament in this instance, since Parliament Hill represents a particular kind of working environment? I think we should discuss this in more detail.
Several other aspects in labour relations would change following the proclamation of parts II and III of the law, for example, sick leave, bereavement leave, maternity leave, leave for care of a child and occupational health and security, all matters which I cannot discuss in detail tonight.
I have spent a few minutes describing possible consequences of the proclamation of parts II and III of the Parliamentary employment and Staff Relations Act. I
think some explanations must still be given on the best way to reach the purpose of Bill C-45. I consider the purpose is to include our employees, while considering our particular work environment. For all of these reasons, I cannot approve of motion M-743, and I thank you.
